# 5.2 Security of the Compilers 

Here, we report the results of the security analysis of each compiler with respect to their base speculative semantics, as indicated in Table 2. Theorem 5 states that each compiler is RSSP w.r.t. its base speculative semantics. Even though we present all results altogether, we remark that each point in Theorem 5 corresponds to an independent secure compilation proof.

Theorem 5 (Compiler Security). The following statements hold:

- (SLS: Fence is secure) $\bigcap_{\text {SLS }} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{SLS}}^{f}: R S S P$
- (R: Retpoline is secure) $\bigcap_{R} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{R}^{\text {rpl }}: R S S P$
- (R: Fence is secure) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{R}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{R}}^{f}: R S S P$
- ( $\mathcal{F}$ : Retpoline is secure) $\bigcap_{j} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{j}^{\text {rpl }}: R S S P$
- ( $\mathcal{F}$ : Retpoline with fence is secure) $\bigcap_{j} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{j}^{\text {rplf }}: R S S P$

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{5}$ Technically, they targeted a While language while we have an assembly-like language $\mu$ Asm. However, the translation is straightforward.

- (S: Fence is secure) $\bigcap_{S} \vdash\llbracket \rrbracket_{S}^{f}: R S S P$
- (B: USLH is secure) $\bigcap_{B}^{c t+d} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{B}^{U S L H}: R S S P$
- (B: SSLH is secure [46]) $\bigcap_{B} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{B}^{S S L H}: R S S P$
- (B: Fence is secure [46]) $\bigcap_{B} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{B}^{f}: R S S P$

# 5.3 Independence of the Compilers 

We now investigate whether our compilers satisfy the Independence in Extension condition. Due to space constraints, we do not report on the Independence and Syntactic Independence for all our compilers and combinations and refer the interested reader to our companion report. Instead, Theorem 6 reports the strongest possible semantics for which we can prove (Syntactic) Independence for each compiler.

Theorem 6 (Compiler Independence). The following statements hold:

- (SLS: Fence Independence) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{SLS}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{SLS}}^{f}: S I$
- (R: Fence Independence) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{R}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{f}: S I$
- (S: Fence Independence) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{R}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{S}}^{f}: S I$ and $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{SLS}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{S}}^{f}: S I$
- (B: Fence Independence) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{R}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{f}: S I$ and $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{SLS}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{f}: S I$
- (B: USLH Independence) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{R}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{S S L H}: I$ and $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{SLS}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{S S L H}: I$
- (B: SSLH Independence) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{R}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{S S L H}: I$ and $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{SLS}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{S S L H}: I$
- (R: Retpoline Independence) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{R}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{r p l}: I$
- (J: Retpoline Independence) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{R}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{J}}^{r p l}: I$
- (J: Retpoline with Fence Independence) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{R}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{J}}^{r p l f}: I$ and $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{SLS}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{J}}^{r p l f}: I$

As stated in Theorem 6, for compilers $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{SLS}}^{f}, \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{f}, \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{S}}^{f}$, and $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{f}$, we directly proved that Syntactic Independence holds even for the strongest possible combined semantics. Given that Syntactic Independence implies Independence (Lemma 1), this allows us to derive Independence results for all these compilers through simple syntactic checks.

For the $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{J}}^{r p l}, \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{J}}^{r p l f}$ and $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{r p l}$ compilers, instead, we have to fall back to a full Independence proof for the strongest semantics. The reason is that these compilers add ret instructions to the code which could interact with R or SLS, i.e., $\operatorname{injInst}\left(\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket\right) \cap \operatorname{specInst}\left(\bigcap_{\mathrm{R}}\right)=\{$ ret $\}$, which violates SI. However, for weaker combinations not including R or SLS, SI applies.

We also remark that Independence does not hold for the retpoline compiler $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{J}}^{r p l}$ and the straightline speculation semantics $\bigcap_{\mathrm{SLS}}$, i.e., $\bigcap_{\mathrm{SLS}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{J}}^{r p l}: I$. The reason is that the ret instructions injected by $\llbracket \rrbracket_{J}^{r p l}$ as part of return trampolines can be speculatively bypassed under $\bigcap_{\mathrm{SLS}}$. The additional speculation barrier injected by the strengthened compiler $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{J}}^{r p l f}$ fixes this issue and allows recovering Independence w.r.t. SLS as well, i.e., $\bigcap_{\mathrm{SLS}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{J}}^{r p l f}: I$.

Finally, for the SLH compilers $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{USLH}}$ and $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{SSLH}}$, we again had to perform full Independence proofs since these compilers inject instructions, which violate SI requirements, for tracking the speculation flag and for masking store and load instructions.

### 5.4 Safe Nesting of the Compilers

The last condition to fulfill for lifting security guarantees is Safe Nesting. Rather than directly proving Safe Nesting, we study which compilers trap speculation according to Definition 11.

Theorem 7 precisely characterize which compilers enjoy this property. Combining Theorem 7 with the fact that trapped speculation implies Safe Nesting (Lemma 2), gives us a precise characterization of which compilers enjoy the Safe Nesting property.

Theorem 7 (Compiler Safe Nesting). The following statements hold:

- (SLS: Fence traps speculation) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{SLS}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{SLS}}^{f}:$ trappedSpec
- (R: Retpoline traps speculation) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{R}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{R}}^{r p l}:$ trappedSpec
- (R: Fence traps speculation) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{R}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{R}}^{f}:$ trappedSpec
- (J: Retpoline traps speculation) $\bigcap_{J} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\rrbracket}^{r p l}:$ trappedSpec
- (J: Retpoline with fence traps speculation) $\bigcap_{J} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{J}^{\text {rplf }}:$ trappedSpec
- (S: Fence traps speculation) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{S}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{S}}^{f}:$ trappedSpec
- (B: Fence traps speculation) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{f}:$ trappedSpec

For all our compilers that rely on inserting spbarr as a countermeasure, proving Trapped Speculation was easy since the speculation barriers immediately stop any speculative transaction. In contrast, for the compilers that inject retpolines, Trapped Speculation follows from the fact that the return-trampoline traps speculation in a loop that does not produce visible events.

Trapped Speculation, however, does not hold for SLH-based countermeasures because these countermeasures do not block speculative execution but rather prevent leaks during speculation. For $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{S S L H}$ and $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{U S L H}$, therefore, we need to directly prove Safe Nesting for each combined semantics, which requires reasoning about all interactions of component semantics. Theorem 8 reports the strongest semantics for which safe nesting holds.

Theorem 8 (Compiler Safe Nesting). The following statements hold:

- (B: SSLH Safe Nesting) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{R}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{S S L H}:$ safeN and $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{SLS}} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{S S L H}:$ safeN
- (B: USLH Safe Nesting) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{R}}^{c t+u l} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{U S L H}:$ safeN and $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{SLS}}^{c t+u l} \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{U S L H}:$ safeN

Intuitively, Safe Nesting holds for the cases in Theorem 8 because the SLH compilers preserve the invariant that the speculation flag is correctly set even when considering speculative transactions caused by semantics like $\bigcap_{\mathrm{S}}$ or $\bigcap_{\mathrm{R}}$.

In contrast, Safe Nesting does not hold for combinations including $\bigcap_{J}$. This follows from the fact that SSLH/USLH compilers do not correctly propagate the value of the speculation flag during indirect jumps. As we state in Theorem 9, this also leads to both $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{S S L H}$ and $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{U S L H}$ being insecure w.r.t. any combination of semantics containing $\bigcap_{J}$ and $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}}$, i.e., any speculative semantics supporting branch and indirect jump speculation.

Theorem 9 (SLH Insecurity w.r.t J). For any speculative semantics $\bigcap$ such that $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j} \subseteq \bigcap$, $\bigcap \nvdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{S S L H}:$ RSNIP and $\bigcap \nvdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{U S L H}:$ RSNIP.

We prove Theorem 9 by finding a source program (which we present in the companion report for space constraints), that after compilation with $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{S S L H} / \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{U S L H}$ still leaks due to indirect jump speculation. The gist of the insecure program is that while the target of the indirect jump is masked by $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{S S L H} / \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{U S L H}$ (to prevent leaks), this does not prevent speculation of indirect jumps that can be used to bypass the instructions tracking the speculation flag inserted by the compiler. Note that this issue could be fixed by relying on hardware support for control-flow-integrity like Intel-CET [49] or ARM-BTI [8], which restrict the targets of indirect jumps to a fixed set of addresses even under speculation. This should be sufficient to ensure that attackers cannot speculatively bypass instructions setting the speculation flags and it should allow us derive Safe Nesting for the SLH compilers w.r.t. combinations including $\bigcap_{J}$. We leave investigating this for future work.

# 5.5 Lifting Security Guarantees 

We conclude our security analysis by using the results from Sections 5.2-5.4 together with Theorem 4 to study how far we can lift the security guarantees provided by each compiler. This allows us to precisely characterize the security of these countermeasures even under stronger semantics.

Theorem 10 summarizes the strongest lifted security guarantees one can derive for each of the studied compilers using our lifting theorem (Theorem 4). After an explanation of the result, we present it visually in Figure 3.

Theorem 10 (Lifted security guarantees). The following statements hold:

- (S: Fence) $\bigcap_{S^{\prime}} \bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+R} \vdash\left\|\|_{S}^{f}: \text { CRSSP and } \bigcap_{S^{\prime}} \bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+S \mid S} \vdash\left\|\cdot\right\|_{S}^{f}: \text { CRSSP }\right.$
- (SLS: Fence) $\bigcap_{\text {SLS }} \bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}} \vdash\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathrm{SLS}}^{f}: \text { CRSSP }$
- (R: Fence) $\bigcap_{R^{\prime}} \bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}} \vdash\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathrm{R}}^{f}: \text { CRSSP }$
- ( $\mathcal{F}$ : Retpoline) $\bigcap_{J^{\prime}} \bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{R}} \vdash\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathrm{J}}^{r p l}: \text { CRSSP }$
- ( $\mathcal{F}$ : Retpoline with fences) $\bigcap_{J^{\prime}} \bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{R}} \vdash\left\|\cdot\right\|_{J}^{\text {rpl }}: \text { CRSSP and } \bigcap_{J^{\prime}} \bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{SLS}} \vdash\left\|\cdot\right\|_{J}^{\text {rplf }}: \text { CRSSP }$
- (R: Retpoline) $\bigcap_{R^{\prime}} \bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}} \vdash\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathrm{R}}^{\text {rpl }}: \text { CRSSP }$
- (B: Fence) $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}^{\prime}} \bigcap_{j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{R}} \vdash\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathrm{B}}^{f}: \text { CRSSP and } \bigcap_{\mathrm{B}^{\prime}} \bigcap_{j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{SLS}} \vdash\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathrm{B}}^{f}: \text { CRSSP }$
- (B: USLH) $\bigcap_{B}^{j+v l} \cdot \bigcap_{S+R}^{j+v l} \vdash\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathrm{B}}^{f} \backslash \mathrm{~L}^{f}: \text { CRSSP and } \bigcap_{B}^{j+v l} \cdot \bigcap_{S+S \mid S}^{j+v l} \vdash\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathrm{B}}^{f: S L H}: \text { CRSSP }$
- (B: SSLH) $\bigcap_{B^{\prime}} \bigcap_{S+R} \vdash\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathrm{B}}^{f S L H}: \text { CRSSP and } \bigcap_{B^{\prime}} \bigcap_{S+S \mid S} \vdash\left\|\cdot\right\|_{B}^{f S L H}: \text { CRSSP }$

For all our compilers except the SLH ones, we can lift the security guarantees up to $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{R}}$ or $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{SLS}}$, the two strongest combined speculative semantics (as shown in Figure 1), i.e., the strongest attacker models considered in our paper.

For the SLH compilers $\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathrm{B}}^{f S L H}$ and $\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathrm{B}}^{f S L H}$, we are able to lift the security guarantees only up to $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{R}}$ and $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{SLS}}$. Lifting the guarantees of $\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathrm{B}}^{f S L H}$ and $\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathrm{B}}^{f S L H}$ to stronger semantics including $\bigcap_{j}$ is not possible because Safe Nesting is not fulfilled (cf. Section 5.4).

Finally, for $\left\|\cdot\right\|_{S S}^{f},\left\|\cdot\right\|_{R}^{f}$ and $\left\|\cdot\right\|_{R}^{\text {rpl }}$, we cannot lift security to both $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{R}}$ and $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{SLS}}$ because we cannot compose $\bigcap_{R}$ and $\bigcap_{\text {SLS }}$ due to limitations of the combination framework (cf. Section 2.4).

We remark that our lifting theorem allowed us to derive strong compiler guarantees, i.e., CRSSP w.r.t. $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{R}}$ or $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+\mathrm{S}+\mathrm{SLS}}$, without requiring new secure compilation proofs, thereby significantly reducing the proving effort. Note that carrying out secure compilation proofs can be complex because each proof requires setting up multiple cross-language relations (for states, values, actions, etc.) [23] as well as defining an invariant that holds for speculation (both in securely-compiled code and in attacker code) [46].

As a concrete example, we use Figure 3 to visualize (1) the effects of Theorem 10 and (2), this lifting for the fence compiler $\left\|\cdot\right\|_{\mathrm{SLS}}^{f}$. With respect to (1), the list of compilers on the left is connected to the strongest semantics to which they can be lifted. With respect to (2), the blue shaded area depicts the semantics to which we can lift the security guarantees using Theorem 4 together with Independence and Safe Nesting. Our lifting approach allowed us to derive secure compilation results for the 7 semantics in the shaded area with only 1 secure compilation proof (for the base semantics $\bigcap_{\text {SLS }}$ ), 1 simple proof of Trapped Speculation, and other 6 simple proofs of Syntactic Independence (by syntactic inspection). Without our approach, proving the same results would have required 7 fully-fledged secure compilation proofs.

![img-9.jpeg](img-9.jpeg)

Fig. 3. On the left is a visualization of Theorem 10, where the list of compilers is connected with a dashed line to the strongest semantic their security is lifted to. On the right, the blue area of the leakage ordering represents where Theorem 4 is applicable for $\llbracket \mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{S} .5}^{f}$. We can lift the security guarantees of $\llbracket \mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{S} .5}^{f}$ from the base semantics $\bigcap_{\mathrm{S} .5}$ to all composed semantics in the highlighted area.

# 6 Discussion 

Scope of the Security Analysis. Lifting the results of our security analysis to real-world CPUs and compilers is only possible to the extent that our models faithfully represent the target systems.

In terms of CPUs and speculative leaks, any information flow in the target CPU that is not captured by our speculative semantics (and their combinations) might invalidate our security proofs in practice. In particular, all speculative semantics from Table 1 consider a commonly-used attacker model [3, 17, 21, 24, 27-29, 46, 53] that captures a cache-based attacker by exposing control-flow and memory accesses along non-speculative and speculative execution paths. Any leaks not reflected in control-flow and memory accesses might, therefore, be missed by our models. Regarding speculation, for the two new semantics modeling speculation over indirect jumps $\left(\bigcap_{j}\right)$ and straight-line speculation $\left(\bigcap_{S .5}\right)$, the main simplification is in the modeling of speculative indirect jumps where we over-approximate the effect of prediction structures (e.g., BTB) by allowing any speculative target. Note, however, that we only support valid instructions in the compiled program as targets of speculative jumps; speculatively jumping in the middle of program instructions is not captured by $\bigcap_{j}$. For the other semantics $\left(\bigcap_{B}, \bigcap_{S}\right.$, and $\bigcap_{B}$ ), we directly employ state-of-the-art models from prior work, whose limitations are discussed in [24, 29].

In terms of compilers, any divergence between our models in Section 5.1 and their actual implementations might, again, invalidate our results. One important simplification of our SLH compilers $\llbracket \frac{3}{2 \mathrm{~B}}^{f S L H}$ and $\llbracket \frac{3}{2 \mathrm{~B}}^{S S L H}$ is that the speculation flag is always stored in a dedicated register. In contrast, the actual SLH implementation in Clang [16] uses a general purpose register for storing the speculation flag which, in some cases, might be spilled to memory. This might result in unexpected leaks in case speculation over store-bypasses $\left(\bigcap_{S}\right)$ might result in loading a stale value for the speculation flag from memory.

Using the Framework. At this point, the reader may wonder how one can use this framework when the next version of Spectre comes out. For example, recent work [43] has discovered that CPUs speculate also on division operations (since this does not lead to actual attacks, we ignored this speculative semantics in our security analysis). Let us indicate a semantics capturing leaks resulting from that speculation over divisions with $\bigcap_{D}$. The ordering of Figure 1 would have many new elements, including a top element $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+5+\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{D}}$. Since none of the considered compilers introduce a division operation, it would be sufficient to prove Syntactic Independence for them, reuse all the theorems from Sections 5.2 and 5.4 and then apply Theorem 4 in order to obtain that those compilers are CRSSP for the new speculative semantics $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}+j+5+\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{D}}$.

Beyond Speculative Leaks. The framework presented in this paper focusses on attacks that arise from speculative executions, but it can be used to reason about the composition of other security properties such as memory safety ( $\bigcap_{M S}$ ) [9] and cryptographic constant time ( $\bigcap_{C T}$, equivalent to our $\bigcap_{N S}$ semantics) [37]. In the case of $\bigcap_{M S}$ and $\bigcap_{C T}$, however, existing semantics that express these leaks can be composed in a much simpler way than speculative semantics, without any nesting. Thus, proving that e.g., countermeasures for $\bigcap_{M S}$ are $C R S S P$ for $\bigcap_{M S+C T}$, only requires reasoning about Independence, because Safe Nesting trivially holds. We leave reasoning about these results (and composing the resulting semantics with the presented ones) as future work.

From Single to Multiple Compilers. We believe this framework can be used beyond reasoning about a single compiler, and it can be employed in order to reason about the application of several Spectre countermeasures. In fact, we speculate that we can use existing results on composing secure compilers [39] to prove that if a compiler $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket_{1}$ is CRSSP with respect to a semantics, and another compiler $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket_{2}$ is CRSSP with respect to the same semantics, then the two can be composed ( $\left.\llbracket \llbracket \llbracket \rrbracket_{2}\right]$ ) and the result is CRSSP with respect to the same semantics. The presented work can then be used to (1) first lift single compiler countermeasures to their strongest semantics and then (2) compose those countermeasures to obtain that the composition is also CRSSP for the strongest semantics. We leave investigating the theory of secure compilation applied to speculative semantics, as well as its application to the results of this paper via points (1) and (2) for future work.

# 7 Related Work 

Speculative Execution Attacks. After Spectre [36] has been disclosed to the public in 2018, researchers have identified many other speculative execution attacks [6, 10, 13, 38, 40, 54, 55]. We refer the reader to Canella et al. [14] for a survey of existing attacks.

Speculative Semantics. There are many semantics capturing the effects of speculatively executed instructions [17, 20, 22, 24, 27, 29, 41, 46, 47, 53]. These semantics differ in the level of microarchitectural details that are modelled (e.g., from program-level models [29] to those closer to simplified CPU designs [27]) and the languages that are used (e.g., from models targeting While languages [46] to those targeting assembly-style languages [29]); see [18] for a survey of speculative semantics.

As indicated in Table 1, our branch speculation semantics $\bigcap_{B}$ is from [29], whereas our storebypass speculation $\bigcap_{S}$ and return misprediction $\bigcap_{R}$ semantics are from [24]. These semantics and our new semantics $\bigcap_{J}$ and $\bigcap_{S \mid S}$ all follow the always-mispredict strategy [29], which explore mispredicted paths for a fixed number of steps before continuing the architectural execution.

Security Properties for speculative leaks. Researchers have proposed many program-level properties for security against speculative leaks, which can be classified in three main groups [18]:
(1) Non-interference definitions ensure the security of speculative and non-speculative instructions. E.g., speculative constant-time [17] extends constant-time to transient instructions as well.

(2) Relative non-interference definitions [19, 27, 29, 30, 51] ensure that transient instructions do not leak more information than non-transient ones. E.g., speculative non-interference [29], which we inherit from the secure compilation framework we build on [46], restricts the information leaked by speculatively executed instructions (without constraining what can be leaked non-speculatively).
(3) Definitions that formalise security as a safety property [46, 47], which may over-approximate definitions from the groups above.

Secure compilation for speculative leaks. Our secure compilation framework extends the work by Patrignani and Guarnieri [46] (which is restricted to branch speculation $\left.\mathfrak{f}_{\mathrm{IB}}\right)$ with support for new speculative semantics and their combinations [24]. In particular, the CRSSP secure compilation criterion from Definition 9 is an extension of the RSSP criterion from [46].

In Section 5, we analyzed Spectre countermeasures implemented in mainstream compilers (or variants of them) or suggested by hardware vendors. Next, we review further countermeasures.

Barthe et al. [11] and Shivakumar et al. [50] extend Jasmin [3, 4] to protect constant-time programs against leaks induced by branch speculation. In contrast, Blade [53] is a countermeasure against Spectre-PHT targeting Wasm [31] which uses a flow-sensitive security-type system to minimize the amount of protect statements (either fences or SLH) needed to secure programs. Differently from our work, which targets speculative non-interference, these works target speculative constant-time.

Swivel [42] is a compiler hardening pass for Wasm that protects against multiple Spectre attacks (Spectre-PHT, Spectre-BTB, and Spectre-RSB). However, it lacks a formal model and security proof.

In concurrent work, Mosier et al. [41] proposed Serberus, a set of compiler passes that-in combination with hardware support (e.g., Intel CET-IBT and a shadow stack for return addresses)offer protection against Spectre-PHT, Spectre-BTB, Spectre-RSB, Spectre-STL and predictive store forwarding [6]. For any whole program satisfying static constant time (a stricter variant of constanttime), Serberus ensures that its compiled counterpart is speculative constant-time. Differently from our security analysis, where we lift secure compilation guarantees from weaker semantics to stronger combined semantics, Serberus' security proof directly targets a speculative semantics incorporating all supported speculation mechanisms. Their proof already targets a semantics at the "top" of the leakage order and does not need lifting (until the discovery of new speculation mechanisms).

Bauer et al. [12] proposes switchpoline, an alternative to retpoline, to protect ARM cores from Spectre-BTB. It transforms indirect calls into direct calls and uses a switch statement to select the correct call target. Interestingly, the authors argue about the importance of compatible countermeasures and ensure that switchpoline is fully compatible with other Spectre countermeasures, which is in line with our Independence property (Definition 7).

# 8 Conclusion 

This paper presented a secure compilation framework for reasoning about the security against leaks introduced by different speculation mechanisms modeled as (combinations of) speculative semantics. In particular, we developed a lifting theorem that allows us to lift a compiler's security guarantees from a weaker base speculative semantics to a stronger extended speculative semantics that accounts for more speculation mechanisms. Additionally, we precisely characterized the security guarantees provided by 9 Spectre-countermeasures implemented in mainstream compilers against 23 different speculative semantics covering combinations of 5 different speculation mechanisms. Our lifting theorem was instrumental in allowing us to precisely characterize each countermeasure's guarantees against all combined semantics without requiring additional secure compilation proofs (beyond the proof of security against each compiler's base semantics).

Frames $B::=\emptyset \mid \bar{n} ; B$

We extend $\mu$ Asm with a notion of components (a unit of compilation) i.e, partial programs $(P)$ and attackers $(A)$. A partial program $P$ defines a list of functions $\bar{F}$ and a list of imports $\bar{I}$, which are all the functions an attacker can define. An attacker $A$ just defines its functions.

Functions $F$ are maps from function names to a pair consisting of the abstract starting label of the function, the code of that function. We define as $f_{\text {set }}$ all the labels of that function which we recover by iterating over the code of the function.

Code of a $\mu$ Asm program p is defined as a sequence of pairs $l_{n}: i$ where $i$ is an instruction and $l_{n}$ is an abstract label drawn from a partially ordered set. We will use $p$ as a partial function from natural numbers to instructions, where $p(n)$ either returns the instruction if the label exists in p or $\perp$. The same abstract label $l_{n}$ cannot be used twice to label two different instructions.

Instructions $i$ include skipping, register assignments, loads, store, indirect jumps, branching, conditional assignments, speculation barriers, calls, and returns. Instructions can contain expressions and values. The former come from the set Regs, containing register identifiers and designated registers pc and sp modelling the program counter and stack pointer respectively, while the latter come from the set Vals, which includes natural numbers and $\perp$.

The Administrative instructions popret and modret $e$ can only be inserted by the compiler and allow for return address manipulation necessary for the Retpoline countermeasure(Appendix O and Appendix R).
$B$ consists of a stack of stacks of natural numbers $n$. These natural numbers represent the return addresses. A new empty stack $\bar{n}$ is created, whenever a context switch between component and attacker happens.

The register file $A$ and the memory $M$ contain mappings from registers and natural numbers to values. The memory consists of a public and a private part. The public one is the positive one and the private one is the negative part. We sometimes write $M^{\mathrm{H}}$ and $M^{\mathrm{L}}$ to indicate the private and public part respectively of memory $M$. The memory is preallocated. This means all locations from 0 up to plus and minus infinity is allocated and initialised to 0 .

A configuration $\sigma$ is a triple $\langle p, m, a\rangle$ containing the program $p$, the memory $m$ and the register file or assignments $a$.

The reason to use these abstract labels $l_{i}$ instead of using natural numbers has to do with compilation. Since our compilation is from $\mu$ Asm to $\mu$ Asm and the compiler inserts new instructions, we run into a lot of trouble with for example jumps or branches. Some jump targets now need to be changed but it is unclear when it needs to change. Abstract labels do not have that problem. When a new instruction is inserted by the compiler, i.e. between $l_{2}$ and $l_{3}$, where $\operatorname{succ}\left(l_{2}\right)=l_{3}$ then we draw a new label $l_{2}^{\prime}$ and insert it into the partial order. If these were natural numbers we would have needed to change all labels of all later instructions. But in this way, we do not change old jump targets.

In the semantics we keep these labels abstract. We will explain this choice in the following section. We note that it is possible to instantiate these labels. See Appendix AB.

Furthermore, in the paper we used $\operatorname{Beh}_{x}(P)$ instead of $\operatorname{Beh}_{x}^{\omega}(P)$ to indicate the behaviour of the program, where $\omega$ is the size of the speculation window.

This additionally means we will always have the correct values when evaluating the expression. (Since the value part of A is updated with each combined step).

# B Leakage Ordering 

Each speculative semantics introduced capture different "attacker models". We follow [28] and and introduce a partial order in terms of leakage between the different semantics.

In particular, we say that semantics $\bigcirc_{1}$ is weaker than another semantics $\bigcirc_{2}$, written $\bigcirc_{1} \sqsubseteq \bigcirc_{2}$ iff $\bigcirc_{2}$ leaks more than $\bigcirc_{1}$, i.e., if any two initial configurations that result in different traces for $\bigcirc_{1}$ also result in different traces for $\bigcirc_{2}$.

## C Contract Compiler and Program Security

Here we define our compiler contract satisfaction and we first introduce the notions of contractaware program security.

In the following sections, we will use the names heaps and memories interchangeably.

## C. 1 General Definitions

We will define $M^{\mathrm{H}}$ for high or private memory and $M^{\mathrm{L}}$ for low or public memory. Again we will use $M^{\mathrm{L}}$ and $M^{\mathrm{H}}$ defined here to mean the public and private part,

$$
\begin{aligned}

& M^{\mathrm{H}}=\left.M\right|_{n<0}

Definition 12 (Dot notation). In the following, we use a dot notation to refer to components of a speculative instance $\Phi_{x}$. For example, we write $\Phi_{x} . \Omega$ to refer to $\Omega$ inside the instance $\Phi_{x}$.

We lift this notation to speculative states $\Sigma_{x}$ in the following way: we write $\Sigma_{x} \cdot \sigma$ to denote the configuration $\sigma$ of the topmost speculative instance $\Phi_{x}$ of the speculative state $\Sigma_{x}$. For example if $\Sigma_{x}=\bar{\Phi}_{x} \cdot \Phi_{x}$ then $\Sigma_{x} . \Omega$ refers to $\Phi_{x} . \Omega$.

A memory $M$ is valid if and only if its private part contains unsafe values. We do not enforce this on the public part too because a program may write a private value in the public heap.

$$

# C. 2 Program level security 

Definition 18 (Speculative Non-interference (SNI)).

$$
\begin{aligned}
\square_{x} \vdash P: S N I \stackrel{\text { def }}{=} \forall P^{\prime} . P^{\prime} & =_{L} P, \forall \overline{\tau_{1}} \in \bigcap_{x}\left(\Omega_{0}(P)\right), \overline{\tau_{2}} \in \bigcap_{x}\left(\Omega_{0}\left(P^{\prime}\right)\right) \\
& \text { if } \overline{\tau_{1}} \uparrow_{n s}=\overline{\tau_{1}} \uparrow_{n s} \text { then } \overline{\tau_{1}}=\overline{\tau_{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

A component $P$ is robustly speculatively non-interferent for a contract $\bigcap_{x}$ if it is SNI for any valid attacker it is linked to (Definition 19).

Definition 19 (Robust Speculative Non-Interference [46]).

$$
\bigcap_{x} \vdash P: R S N I \stackrel{\text { def }}{=} \forall A \text { if } \vdash A: \text { atk then } \vdash A[P]: S N I
$$

Definition 20 (Speculative Safety (SS)).

$$
\bigcap_{x} \vdash P: S S \stackrel{\text { def }}{=} \forall \overline{\tau^{\sigma}} \in \bigcap_{x}(P) . \forall \tau^{\sigma} \in \overline{\tau^{\sigma}} . \sigma \equiv S
$$

A component is robustly speculatively safe (RSS) for a spec. semantics $\bigcap_{x}$ if it is SS no matter what attacker it is linked against (SS).

Definition 21 ( Robust Speculative Safety [46]).

$$
\bigcap_{x} \vdash P: R S S \stackrel{\text { def }}{=} \forall A \text {. if } \vdash A: \text { atk then } \bigcap_{x} \vdash A[P]: S S
$$

Since there is no speculation in $L$ both definitions are trivially satisfied.
Theorem 11 (SS AND SNI hold FOR ALL SOURCE PROGRAMS).

$$
\forall P \in L . \bigcap_{N S} \vdash P: S S \text { and } \bigcap_{N S} \vdash P: S N I
$$

Proof. This trivially holds from (1) programs in $L$ produce only actions labelled with $S$ (for SS, and (2) traces are identical to their non-speculative projection for programs $L$ (for $\bigcap_{N S}$ ).

## C. 3 Compiler-level Security

A compiler preserves RSS for a given contract $\bigcap_{x}$ if given a source component that is RSS, the compiled counterpart is also RSS (RSSP).

Definition 22 (Robust speculative safety preservation [46] (RSSP)). $\bigcap_{x} \vdash\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P \stackrel{\text { def }}{=} \forall P \in$ L. if $\bigcap_{N S} \vdash P: R S S$ then $\bigcap_{x} \vdash \llbracket P \rrbracket: R S S$

Similarly, a compiler preserves RSNI for a given contract $\bigcap_{x}$ if given a source component that is RSNI, the compiled counterpart is also RSNI.

Definition 23 (Robust speculative non-interference preservation [46] (RSNIP)). $\bigcap_{x} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S N I P \stackrel{\text { def }}{=}$ $\forall P \in L$. if $\bigcap_{N S} \vdash P: R S N I$ then $\bigcap_{x} \vdash \llbracket P \rrbracket: R S N I$

Furthermore, we can also specify multiple contract security in the obvious way.
We can recover the original definitions of Patrignani and Guarnieri [46] by specifying contracts $\mathfrak{C}_{N S}$ and $\mathfrak{C}_{\mathrm{R}}$ for their semantics, capturing non-speculative execution and speculation on branch instructions in their languages.

Given that contracts form a partial order $\square$, it follows that a compiler preserving the security for a stronger contract also implies that the same compiler preserves security even for a weaker contract (Corollary 3).

Corollary 3 (Leakage Ordering and RSNIP). If $\bigcap_{1} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S N I P$ and $\bigcap_{2} \square \bigcap_{1}$ then $\bigcap_{2} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S N I P$

Similarly, if a compiler is not secure for a weaker contract, it also is not secure for the stronger contract as well.
Corollary 4 ([Leakage ordering and RSNIP Negative). If $\bigcap_{1} \vDash\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S N I P$ and $\bigcap_{1} \sqsubset \bigcap_{2}$ then $\bigcap_{2} \vDash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S N I P$

Expansion of RSSPfor RSS yields:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \forall P \text {. if } \forall A \cdot \forall \overline{r^{\sigma}} \in \operatorname{Beh}(A[P]), \forall \tau^{\sigma} \in \overline{r^{\sigma}} \cdot \sigma \equiv S \\
& \text { then } \forall A \cdot \forall \overline{r^{t}} \in \bigcap_{N S}\left(A\left[\llbracket P \rrbracket\right]\right) \cdot \forall \tau^{t} \in \overline{r^{t}} \cdot t \equiv S
\end{aligned}
$$

We say that a source and a target trace are related $(\approx)$ if the latter contains the source trace plus interleavings of only safe actions. The trace relation relies on a relation on actions which in turn relies on a relation on values and heaps.

The last two are compiler-dependent, so they are presented later.

# N. 1 Compilation of instructions 

Note that the compilation of instructions is a function from programs to programs. Since $l: i$ belongs to the syntactic category of programs. This means stuff like $\mathrm{p}(\mathrm{l})=\llbracket i \rrbracket_{\mathrm{S}}^{f}$ does not make much sense because $p(l)$ is a partial function from labels to instructions. Thus, when we state $1: \mathrm{i}=\llbracket i \rrbracket_{\mathrm{S}}^{f}: \llbracket i \rrbracket_{\mathrm{S}}^{f}$ it should be $1: \mathrm{i}=\llbracket l: i \rrbracket_{\mathrm{S}}^{f}$. However, for example for a store instruction, the compiler will insert an lfence. Thus, now we have a sequence. $\llbracket l: i \rrbracket_{\mathrm{S}}^{f}=p_{1} ; p_{2}$ which cannot be equal. Thus, in this case we can state this:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\llbracket l: i \rrbracket_{\mathrm{S}}^{f} & =p_{\mathrm{c}} \\
\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{c}} & =1: \mathrm{i} ; \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{c}}^{\prime} \\

\end{aligned}
$$

Recovering the relation to $1: i$. This means, that in the compiled program, we need to handle all steps introduced by the compilation in one big step. Otherwise, this relation will not hold, because we would be somewhere in $\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{c}}^{\prime}$. # O $j$ : The Retpoline compiler 

Retpoline is a specific code sequence that replaces indirect jumps by a "return trampoline". Conceptually retpoline looks like this:

```
call retpoline_rax
    ...
retpoline_rax:
l_0 : call LIND1
LIND0:
l_1 : skip
l_2 : spbarr
l_3 : jmp l_1
LIND1
l_4 : modret rax
l_5 : ret
```

Listing 1. Code on the left and the compiled program with the retpoline countermeasure on the right.

We also assume that the labels used for this new thunk are not used in the program. In $l_{4}$ we modify the return address to be the content of the rax register, which was the initial jump goal. Thus the ret instruction at the end returns to the target of the original indirect jump.

Notice, that this retpoline is constructed for an indirect jump targeting the rax register. We need to create additional functions for each indirect jump. This is option thunk.

Thus, we assume a pass before the retpoline pass that for each indirect jump in the program, adds a new function with a fresh name retpo_trg_l for the indirect jump at location $l$. This function for jmp $e$ consists of:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& l^{\prime}: \text { modret }\llbracket e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} \\
& l^{\prime \prime}: \text { ret }
\end{aligned}
$$

where $l^{\prime}$ and $l^{\prime \prime}$ are freshly chosen labels.

We are now ready to state the compiler:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \llbracket M ; \bar{F} ; \bar{I} \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=\llbracket M \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} ; \llbracket \bar{F} \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} ; \llbracket \llbracket \llbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} \\
& \llbracket \emptyset \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=\emptyset \\
& \llbracket \bar{I} \cdot f \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=\llbracket \llbracket \llbracket_{j}^{\rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}} \cdot \llbracket f \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} \\
& \llbracket M ;-n \mapsto v: U \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=\llbracket M \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} ;-\llbracket n \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} \mapsto \llbracket v \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}: \mathrm{U} \\
& \llbracket p_{1} ; p_{2} \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=\llbracket p_{1} \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} ; \llbracket p_{2} \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} \\
& \llbracket l: i \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=\llbracket l \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} \cdot \llbracket i \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} \text { if } i \neq \text { jmp } \\
& \llbracket \text { skip } \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=\text { skip } \\
& \llbracket x \leftarrow e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=x \leftarrow \llbracket e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} \\
& \llbracket x \stackrel{e^{r_{2}}}{\leftarrow} e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=x \stackrel{\llbracket e^{r} \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}}{\llbracket e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}} \llbracket e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} \\
& \llbracket \text { load }_{p r v} x, e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=\text { load }_{\mathrm{prv}} \mathrm{x}, \llbracket e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} \\
& \llbracket \text { load } x, e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=\text { load } \mathrm{x}, \llbracket e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} \\
& \llbracket \text { store } x, e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=\text { store } \mathrm{x}, \llbracket e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} \\
& \llbracket \text { store }_{p r v} x, e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=\text { store }_{\mathrm{prv}} \mathrm{x}, \llbracket e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} \\
& \llbracket \text { beqz } x, l^{\prime} \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=\text { beqz } \mathrm{x}, \llbracket l^{\prime} \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} \\
& \llbracket \text { call } f \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=\text { call } f \text { Here } f \text { is a function name } \\
& \llbracket \operatorname{ret} \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=\text { ret } \\
& \llbracket l: \text { jmp } e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=1: \text { jmp } \llbracket e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} \text { if jmp } e \text { not indirect } \\

\end{aligned}

## S SLS: THE SLS Compiler for Straighline-Speculation

A compiler against Straightline speculation inserts an int3 instruction, which is an interrupt and stops speculation. We model this by fence instruction. The interrupt instruction is used because it is only 1 byte and not 3 like for the fence. These instructions are architecturally never executed, because the control flow diverted before, so they have no additional cost except for an increase in binary size.

Most interestingly, this kind of speculation depends on the program's layout because it executes the instructions following a return.

Again, this is a vulnerability only made visible by our assembly-like semantics. In higher-level language models, there is nothing after a return. So it is hard to model the vulnerability and the countermeasure.

# T The USLH Compiler 

Here we describe ultimate speculative-load-hardening (USLH) by Zhang et al. [56]. The authors show that variable time instructions can be used to leak a secret.

This is not captured in the model of Patrignani and Guarnieri [46], because variable time latency is not captured in the attacker model that Patrignani and Guarnieri [46] use.

While the authors of [56] have a proof that their uslh is secure (w.r.t. a notion of speculative constant time), their proof is not robust in our sense.

To model variable time latency instructions, we extend our model of $\mu$ Asm with a second assignment operation for variable time instructions. This new assignment operations leaks the operands of the operation.

We note that the base for this compiler is the strong-slh compiler $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{SSLH}}$ of [46] without the additional rule for variable time latency instructions. Thus, the compiler $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{USLH}}$ and $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{SSLH}}$ only differ for variable time latency instructions and we do not present $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{SSLH}}$ separately.

The compiler uses a scratch registers to save the immediate values and we reserve a register $r_{s l h}$ as a speculation flag. This register is initially set to false and is set to true when speculation starts. Note, that we assume that this register is not used by the program and only inserted by the compiler.

We need to be careful when compiling the beqz instruction. Because we operate on the $\mu$ Asm level we actually do not have access to both branches when just looking at the instruction. We know that the instructions after the branch instruction are the ones of the branch is not taken. However, we do not know where the label $l$ in the program is for the instruction beqz $x, l$. However, we need the code at this position as well to correctly update the predicate bit $r_{s l h}$ (Note that the same would have to be done for a fence compiler since you need to protect both branches). In general, this means that the compilation of a beqz instruction is a non-local transformation. The idea is to redirect the original branch target. That is achieved by the label $l_{\text {new }}$ which first updates the register $r_{s l h}$ and then jumps to the original target $l^{\prime}$ when the branch is taken. If the branch is not taken then we go to $l_{2}$ and update $r_{s l h}$. A jump to next $(l)$ allows us to access the original "else" branch of the conditional. All in all, this way we achieved to update $r_{s l h}$ in both parts of the

branches without needing to modify other parts of the program. This is a local transformation for the branch.

# T. 5 Another (faulty) USLH Compiler 

We leave it here because we think it is insightful. Previously, we used this version of the compiler

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \llbracket l: l \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{LSLH}}=l: r_{s l h} \leftarrow r_{s l h} \vee \neg r_{s c r a t c h} \text { if } l \in \mathcal{B}_{l} \\
& \llbracket l^{\prime}: l \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{LSLH}} \\
& \llbracket x \leftarrow e \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{LSLH}}=r_{\text {scratch }} \leftarrow \llbracket e \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{LSLH}} \\
& r_{\text {scratch }} \stackrel{r_{\text {slh }}{ } 0}{\leftarrow} 0 \\
& x \leftarrow r_{\text {scratch }} \\
& \llbracket \text { beqz } x, l^{\prime} \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mathrm{LSLH}}=r_{\text {scratch }} \leftarrow x \\
& r_{\text {scratch }} \stackrel{r_{\text {slh }}{ } 0}{\leftarrow} 0 \\
& \text { beqz } r_{\text {scratch }}, l^{\prime} \\
& l_{1}: r_{s l h} \leftarrow r_{s l h} \vee r_{\text {scratch }}
\end{aligned}
$$

We define the branch label set as $\mathcal{B}_{l}:=\{l \mid \forall i \in p, i=\operatorname{beqz} x, l\}$.
However, this has certain problems. Consider a do while loop.

![table_3](table_3)

Since $r_{s l h}=$ false but $r_{\text {scratch }}=5=$ false we get that $r_{s l h}=$ false $\vee \neg$ false $=$ true when executing $l_{3}$ which is the countermeasure introduced because of the branch later on. Even though no speculation

is happening! The problem is that the use of $r_{\text {scratch }}$ is not guarded which is normally not a problem because every instruction overwrites the value in the compiler. However, in the case for the branch target, we do not know if the branch instruction is executed right before and as we can see, it is not the only way to reach the branch target in a program.

So this branch is reachable from two independent positions in the code, i.e. the start of the do while loop and then when the branch is executed. That is why we need to reset the value of the scratch register to 0 (which equals true) so that we do not accidentally pull up the value of $r_{\text {slh }}$. The fix looks like this:
![img-60.jpeg](img-60.jpeg)

Again the problem is that one of the branches is not related to the branch instruction itself and can be reached before the branch is executed. The branch construct is stronger than a normal if, which makes sense.

## V. 3 Join and Projection on instances / states

We define the a join operator $\sqcup_{x y}$ on instances:

$$
\bigsqcup_{x y}:\left(\Phi_{x}, \Phi_{y}\right) \mapsto \Phi_{x y}
$$

Note, that the join operations is only defined iff all the components $c$ in $\Phi_{x} \cap \Phi_{y}$ are equal, i.e. $\forall c \in \Phi_{x} \cap \Phi_{y} \cdot \Phi_{x} \cdot c=\Phi_{y} \cdot c$.

Furthermore, we define projection functions $\uparrow_{x y}$ as the inverse of the join function:

$$
\uparrow_{x y}: \Phi_{x y} \mapsto\left(\Phi_{x}, \Phi_{y}\right)
$$

We require that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqcup_{x y}\left(\Phi_{x y} \uparrow_{x y}\right) & =\Phi_{x y} \\
\left(\sqcup_{x y}\left(\Phi_{x}, \Phi_{y}\right)\right) \uparrow_{x y} & =\left(\Phi_{x}, \Phi_{y}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we will define two more specific projection $\uparrow_{x y}^{x}$ and $\uparrow_{x y}^{y}$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \uparrow_{x y}^{x}: \Phi_{x y} \mapsto \Phi_{x} \\
& \uparrow_{x y}^{y}: \Phi_{x y} \mapsto \Phi_{y}
\end{aligned}
$$

They are defined as the first and second projection of the generated pair from $\uparrow_{x y}$.

Definition 31 (Well-formed composition). A composition $\bigcirc_{x y}$ of two speculative contracts $\bigcirc_{x}$ and $\bigcirc_{y}$ is well-formed, denoted with $\vdash \bigcirc_{x y}: W F C$ if:
(1) (Confluence) Whenever $\Sigma_{x y} \stackrel{\tau}{\rightarrow} \bigcirc_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}$ and $\Sigma_{x y} \stackrel{\tau}{\rightarrow} \bigcirc_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$, then $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}=\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$ and $\tau=\tau^{\prime}$.
(2) (Projection preservation) For all programs $p, B e h_{x}^{\omega}(p)=B e h_{x y}^{\omega}(p) \uparrow_{x y}^{x}$ and $B e h_{y}^{\omega}(p)=B e h_{x y}^{\omega}(p) \uparrow_{x y}^{y}$.
(3) (Relation Preservation) If $\Sigma_{x} \stackrel{\tau}{\rightarrow} \Sigma_{x}^{\prime} \Sigma_{x}^{\prime}$ and $\Sigma_{x} \approx_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger}$ then there exists $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$ such that $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger} \stackrel{\tau}{\rightarrow} \bigcirc_{x y}$ $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$ and $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime} \approx_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$.

# W Lifting Security Guarantees to stronger attackers 

Here we present results that lift guarantees of a compiler for a specific semantics to guarantees about the combination of different spec. semantics.

The running example that we will use is a combination of Spectre v2 and Spectre v5. The retpoline countermeasure $\frac{p}{8} \frac{\gamma^{p l}}{2}$ introduces new ret instructions into the compiled code. These ret instructions are a source of speculation for Spectre v5. Thus, the natural question to ask is, if the compiled program introduces new Spectre v5 vulnerabilities into the code.

Afterwards, we define two properties Syn, Independence and Trapped Speculation which are simpler to prove and imply the stronger conditions.

## W. 1 Interplay of semantics

Figure 4 depicts two portions of traces produced when executing a program under the composed semantics $\bigcirc_{x+y}$. The first trace (top) starts with a speculative transaction from semantics $\bigcirc_{x}$ (highlighted in red and starting with action start ${ }_{x}$ ). Inside the red speculative transaction, there is a nested speculative transaction from semantics $\bigcirc_{y}$ (highlighted in green, starting with action $\operatorname{start}_{y}$ and ending with action $\mathrm{rlb}_{y}$ ). After the termination of the nested transaction, the outer red transaction continues until the end of its speculative window (action $\mathrm{rlb}_{x}$ ). Dually, the second

trace (bottom) starts with a speculative transaction from $\bigcap_{y}$ followed by a nested transaction from $\bigcap_{x}$.

Thus, there are three different regions that might results in leaks:

- Region 1: the speculative transaction started by $\bigcap_{x}$ (highlighted in red),
- Region 2: the speculative transaction started by $\bigcap_{y}$ (highlighted in blue), and
- Region 3: the nested transactions (highlighted in green).

While leaks in region 1 are fixed by proving the security of a compiler for spec. semantics $\bigcap_{x}$, i.e., $\bigcap_{x} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P$, we need additional conditions to ensure the absence of leaks in Regions 2 and 3.

Thus, we introduce the notions of Independence w.r.t. a spec. semantics $\bigcap_{y}$ and Safe Nesting which ensure the absence of leaks in Regions 2 and 3 respectively.

# W. 2 Independence 

A compiler $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket$ for the origin semantics $\bigcap_{x}$ is called independent for the extension semantics $\bigcap_{y}$ iff the compiler does not introduce further leaks under the extension semantics $\bigcap_{y}$.

Definition 32 (Independence in extension). $\bigcap_{y} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: I \stackrel{\text { def }}{=} \forall p . \bigcap_{y} \vdash p: R S S \Longrightarrow \bigcap_{y} \vdash \llbracket p \rrbracket: R S S$
Corollary 5 (Self Independence). If $\bigcap_{x} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P$ then
$\bigcap_{x} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: I$
Proof. Assume we have $\bigcap_{x} \vdash P:$ RSS. We now need to show that $\bigcap_{x} \vdash \llbracket P \rrbracket$ : RSS.
Unfolding $\bigcap_{x} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P$ we get $\bigcap_{N S} \vdash P$ : RSS then $\bigcap_{x} \vdash \llbracket P \rrbracket$ : RSS
Because of Theorem 11 (SS and SNI hold for all source programs) we have $\bigcap_{N S} \vdash P$ : RSS and thus can use $\bigcap_{x} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P$ to get $\bigcap_{x} \vdash \llbracket P \rrbracket$ : RSS.

With this, we are done.

## W. 3 Safe Nesting

The last we need to talk about nesting. For that we define a predicate safe nesting
Definition 33 (Safe nested Speculation). Given a program $p$, we say that the program has safe nesting, written

$$
\bigcap_{x+y} \vdash p: \operatorname{safe} N
$$

, iff

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \bigcap_{x+y} \vdash P: \operatorname{safe} N \stackrel{\text { def }}{=} \forall \bar{\tau} \in \operatorname{Beh}_{x y}^{\mathrm{er}}(P), \text { if } \\
& \text { (1) } \operatorname{start}_{a} \cdot \bar{\tau}^{\prime} \cdot \mathrm{rlb}_{a} \text { is a subtrace of } \bar{\tau} \\
& \text { (2) } \operatorname{start}_{b} \cdot \bar{\tau}^{\prime \prime} \cdot \mathrm{rlb}_{b} \text { is a subtrace of } \bar{\tau}^{\prime} \\
& \text { then } \vdash \bar{\tau}^{\prime \prime}: \text { safe } \\
& \text { where } a \in\{x, y\} \text { and } b \in\{x, y\} \backslash\{a\}
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we say that a compiler satisfies the Safe Nested Speculation property, written $\bigcap_{x+y} \vdash$ $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket$ : safeN, iff all its compiled programs satisfy Definition 33, i.e., $\forall p . \bigcap_{x+y} \vdash \llbracket p \rrbracket$ : safeN.

## W. 4 Conditional Robust Speculative Safety

Often compilers implementing Spectre countermeasures are developed to prevent leaks introduced by a specific speculation mechanism.
$R S S P$ is too strict as a criterion here, since it cannot distinguish between the different speculation mechanisms that might induce the leak. To account for this, we propose a new secure compilation

criterion called Conditional Robust Speculative Safety Preservation (CRSSP, Definition 34). As the name indicates, CRSSP is a variant of RSSP that restricts RSS preservation only to those programs that do not contain leaks caused only by the additional mechanisms.
Definition 34 (Conditional Robust Speculative Safety Preservation (CRSSP)). $\bigcirc_{x}, \bigcirc_{y} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket$ : $C R S S P \stackrel{\text { def }}{=} \forall P \in L$. if $\bigcap_{N S} \vdash P: R S S$ and $\bigcap_{y} \vdash P: R S S$ then $\bigcap_{x+y} \vdash \llbracket P \rrbracket: R S S$

# W. 5 Lifted Compiler Preservation 

Using Independence and Safe Nesting, we are now ready to state our main theorem:
Theorem 52 (Lifted Compiler Preservation). If $\bigcap_{x} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P$ and $\bigcap_{y} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: I$ and $\bigcap_{x+y} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket:$ safeN and $\vdash \bigcap_{x+y}: W F C$ then $\bigcap_{x}, \bigcap_{y} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: C R S S P$
Proof. Assume a program $P$ and $\bigcap_{N S} \vdash P$ : RSS and $\bigcap_{y} \vdash P$ : RSS. We need to show $\bigcap_{x+y} \vdash$ $\llbracket P \rrbracket$ : RSS.

Let us first collect we know:
From $\bigcap_{y} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: I$ and $\bigcap_{y} \vdash P$ : RSS we get $\bigcap_{y} \vdash \llbracket P \rrbracket$ : RSS.
From $\bigcap_{N S} \vdash P$ : RSS and $\bigcap_{x} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket$ : $R S S P$ we get $\bigcap_{x} \vdash \llbracket P \rrbracket$ : RSS.
By $\bigcap_{x+y} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket$ : safeN we know that nested speculative actions are safe.
$\bar{\tau}$ that is generated for $\bigcap_{x y}$ for $\llbracket P \rrbracket$.
The non-speculative parts are safe by definition. They cannot produce unsafe actions.
Lets look at the speculative parts of $\bar{\tau}$.

## Inside a speculation of $\mathbf{x}$

Now lets look at the trace actions that can be generated Now lets look at the subtraces $\bar{\tau}^{\prime}$ :
$\bar{\tau}^{\prime}=$ start $_{y}$ ctr $\cdot \bar{\tau}^{\prime \prime} \cdot \mathrm{rlb}_{y}$ ctr
Thus, we have nesting of speculative transactions. By $\bigcap_{x+y} \vdash \llbracket p \rrbracket$ : safeN we know that nesting is safe.

## otherwise

From above, we have $\bigcap_{x} \vdash \llbracket P \rrbracket$ : RSS. Together with Projection Preservation of $\vdash \bigcap_{x+y}$ : $W F C$ we know that these actions are safe

Now lets look at the trace actions that can be generated

From above, we have $\bigcap_{y} \vdash \llbracket P \rrbracket$ : RSS (Independence).
We are now done.
This means our compilers can be embedded under even stronger attackers without needing to worry if there are bad interactions with the inserted instructions of the compiler and other speculative variants. Essentially, our well-formed compilers are secure even under a stronger attacker that allows for more speculation.

## W. 7 Syntactic Independence

Using our running example of Spectre v2 and Spectre v5 and their combination, we can see that the newly introduced ret instructions could interact with Spectre v5 in the combination. That is why we have the second condition of well-formedness. However, what is with the other direction? The Spectre v5 compiler $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket_{0}^{f}$ inserts only fence instructions into the program.

This is important since many of the compilers we defined do not have interactions with other speculative mechanisms. Thus, we do not need to do a full proof that they do not interact but instead can use this easier way to fulfil the condition

Before formalizing SI, we introduce some notation. Given a compiler $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket$, we denote by injInst( $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket$ ) the set of instructions that the compiler inserts during compilation. For instance, for a simple compiler $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{f}$ that inserts spbarr instructions after branch instruction to prevent speculation [46], injInst( $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{f}$ ) is the set $\{$ spbarr $\}$. Given a semantics $\bigcirc$, we denote by specInst( $\bigcirc$ ) the set of instructions that trigger speculation in $\bigcirc$. For example, beqz $x, l$ for $\bigcirc_{B}$.

Definition 37 (Syntactic Independence). A compiler $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket$ is syntactically independent for a contract $\bigcirc$, written $\vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: S l$, iff injInst $\left(\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket\right) \cap \operatorname{specInst}(\bigcirc)=\emptyset$ and injInst $\left(\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket\right) \cap\{$ beqz, jmp, store, load, $\left.\leftarrow\right\}=\emptyset$.

Corollary 6. If

(1) $\bigcap_{y} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: S I$

Then
(1) $\bigcap_{y} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: I$

Proof. Assume we have a program $p$ with $\bigcap_{y} \vdash p:$ RSS.
Because of $\vdash \bigcap_{y}: S I$, we know that the compiler does not insert any instructions related to speculation of $\bigcap_{y}$. Thus, no additional speculation related to $\bigcap_{y}$ is introduced by the compiler. Since the initial program was secure for $\bigcap_{y}$ and no additional speculation is added during compilation, we have $\bigcap_{y} \vdash \llbracket p \rrbracket:$ RSS

# W. 8 Non-Trivial Independence Results 

Here, we provide the results for the Independence results $I$ in the table above.
We show the Independence result only for the "smallest" contract where the proof is necessary. In all combined contracts the same proof can be used. For example, if we have proven $\bigcap_{i 1} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}: I$ then we have the same proof for $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B} \neq \mathrm{R}} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}: I$ as well.

Lemma 70. $\bigcap_{i 1} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}: I$
Proof. By definition of Independence, we know that forall programs $p$ that $\bigcap_{i 1} \vdash p:$ RSS. Thus, we are only interested in newly added ret instructions from the compiler $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}$. These are only added when an indirect jump is encountered and is replaced with the following sequence.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \llbracket l: \text { jmp } e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}=l^{\prime}: \text { call retpo_trg_l Rule R:AM-Call } \\
& l_{1}^{\prime}: \text { skip Rule R:AM-NoSpec-epsilon } \\
& l_{2}^{\prime}: \text { spbarr } \\
& l_{3}^{\prime}: \text { jmp } l_{1}^{\prime} \\
& l_{4}^{\prime}: \text { modret } \llbracket e \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l} \text { Rule R:AM-NoSpec-epsilon } \\
& l_{5}^{\prime}: \text { ret Rule R:AM-Ret-Spec }
\end{aligned}
$$

Here we annotated, which rule is used from the $\bigcap_{i 1}$ semantics when this code sequence is executed in the interesting case when speculation is stated. Otherwise, this sequence is trivially secure.

When speculation is started, the topmost entry of the $\mathbb{R}$ is taken, which is $l_{1}^{\prime}$, because the last call instruction was the one in $l^{\prime}$. The code sequence at $l_{1}^{\prime}, l_{2}^{\prime}$ and $l_{3}^{\prime}$ is an infinite loop containing a barrier instruction. Thus, speculation is trapped and stopped at $l_{2}^{\prime}$. This causes a rollback to occur. Most importantly, during speculation no memory is accessed and no observations apart from the rollback were made. Thus, the speculation is secure.

Since this is the only additional source of speculation, we have that $\bigcap_{i 1} \vdash \llbracket p \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}:$ RSS.
Next, we provide the Independence result for the extended retpoline compiler $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l f}$.
Lemma 71. $\bigcap_{\text {St.S }} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l f}: I$
Proof. By definition of Independence, we know that for all programs $p$ that $\bigcap_{\text {St.S }} \vdash p:$ RSS. Thus, we are only interested in newly added ret instructions from the compiler $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l f}$. These are only added when an indirect jump is encountered and is replaced with the following sequence.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \llbracket l: \text { jmp } e \rrbracket_{j}^{\text {rpl }}=l^{\prime} \text { : call retpo_trg_l Rule SLS:AM-NoSpec-action } \\
& l_{1}^{\prime} \text { : skip Rule SLS:AM-NoSpec-epsilon } \\
& l_{2}^{\prime} \text { : spbarr } \\
& l_{3}^{\prime}: \text { jmp } l_{1}^{\prime} \\
& l_{4}^{\prime}: \text { modret } \llbracket e \rrbracket_{j}^{\text {rpl }} \text { Rule SLS:AM-NoSpec-epsilon } \\
& l_{5}^{\prime} \text { : ret Rule SLS:AM-Ret-Spec } \\
& l_{6}^{\prime} \text { : spbarr }
\end{aligned}
$$

When speculation is started with Rule SLS:AM-Ret-Spec, it is immediately stopped by the additional barrier in $l_{6}^{\prime}$. Thus, the additional speculation is secure.
