## X Speculative Safety Combined

We will write $\vdash \bigcap_{x y}: W F C_{n}$ to refer to the n-th fact of Definition 31 (Well-formed composition)
From these conditions, we can generally derive that SS overapproximates SNI for a general well-formed combination (Theorem 53 (SS implies SNI)).

Theorem 53 (SS implies SNI). If
(1) $\bigcap_{x y} \vdash P: S S$

Then

$$
I \bigcap_{x y} \vdash P: S N I
$$

Proof. Let $P$ be an arbitrary program such that $\bigcap_{x y} \vdash P$ : SS. Proof by contradiction.
Assume that $\bigcap_{x y} \vdash P$ : SNI does not hold. That is, there is another program $P^{\prime}$ and traces $\overline{\tau_{1}} \in \operatorname{Beh}\left(\Omega_{0}(P)\right)$ and $\overline{\tau_{2}} \in \operatorname{Beh}\left(\Omega_{0}\left(P^{\prime}\right)\right)$ such that $P={ }_{L} P^{\prime}, \overline{\tau_{1}} \upharpoonright_{n s}=\overline{\tau_{2}} \upharpoonright_{n s}$, and $\overline{\tau_{1}} \neq \overline{\tau_{2}}$.

Since $\overline{\tau_{1}} \in \operatorname{Beh}\left(\Omega_{0}(\mathbf{P})\right)$ we have $\mathbf{P} \bigcap_{\mathrm{xy}}^{\mathrm{c} \dagger} \overline{\tau^{t}}$ and by Rule xy:AM-Trace we know that there exists $\Sigma_{x y}^{F}$ such that $\Sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^{0}(\mathbf{P}) \Downarrow_{\mathrm{xy}}^{\overline{\tau_{1}^{\prime}}} \Sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^{\mathrm{F}}$. Similarly, we get $\Sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^{0}\left(\mathbf{P}^{\prime}\right) \Downarrow_{\mathrm{xy}}^{\overline{\tau_{2}}} \Sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^{\mathrm{F}^{\prime}}$.

Combined with the fact that $\overline{\tau_{1}} \neq \overline{\tau_{2}}$, it follows that there exists speculative states $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger}, \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger \dagger}, \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}$, $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$ and sequences of observations $\bar{\tau}, \bar{\tau}_{\text {end }}, \bar{\tau}_{\text {end }}^{\prime}, \tau^{t}, \alpha^{\prime t^{\prime}}$ such that $\tau^{t} \neq \alpha^{\prime t^{\prime}}$ and:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^{0}(\mathbf{P}) \Downarrow_{\mathrm{xy}}^{\bar{\tau}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger} \underset{\longrightarrow}{\stackrel{\tau^{\prime}}{\rightleftarrows}} \underset{\longrightarrow}{\longrightarrow} \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger \dagger} \Downarrow_{\mathrm{xy}}^{\bar{\tau}_{\text {end }}} \Sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^{\mathrm{F}} \\
& \Sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^{0}\left(\mathbf{P}^{\prime}\right) \Downarrow_{\mathrm{xy}}^{\bar{\tau}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime} \stackrel{\alpha^{\prime \prime}}{\longrightarrow} \underset{\longrightarrow}{\longrightarrow} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime} \Downarrow_{\mathrm{xy}}^{\bar{\tau}^{\prime}} \Sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}^{\mathrm{F}^{\prime}}
\end{aligned}
$$

From $\bigcap_{x y} \vdash P: S S$ we get that $\vdash \overline{\tau_{1}}:$ safe.
From Lemma 73 (Comb : Low-equivalent programs have low-equivalent initial states) we get $\Sigma_{x y}^{0}(P) \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{0}\left(P^{\prime}\right)$.

Using Lemma 72 (Comb: Steps of $\Downarrow_{x y}$ with safe observations preserve Safe-equivalence) on $\Sigma_{x y}^{0}(P) \Downarrow_{x y}^{\bar{\tau}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger}$ we get $\Sigma_{x y}^{0}\left(P^{\prime}\right) \Downarrow_{x y}^{\bar{\tau}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime \prime}$ and $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime \prime}$.

By $\vdash \bigcap_{x y}: W F C_{1}$ (Confluence) we know that $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}=\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime \prime}$ and thus we have $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$.
We know apply $\vdash \bigcap_{x y}: W F C_{3}$ (Relation Preservation) on $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger} \stackrel{\tau^{\prime}}{\longrightarrow} \underset{\longrightarrow}{\longrightarrow} \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger \dagger}$ and $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}$ and get $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime} \underset{\longrightarrow}{\stackrel{\tau^{\prime}}{\rightleftarrows}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime \prime}$.

Again, by Confluence we know that $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}=\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime \prime \prime}$.
However, now we have that the same observation $\tau^{t}$ is made in both executions contradicting our initial assumption

From this we can follow that RSS implies RSNI as well.
Theorem 54 (RSS implies RSNI). If
(1) $\bigcap_{x y} \vdash P: R S S$

Then

$$
I \bigcap_{x y} \vdash P: R S N I
$$

Proof. Unfolding the definition of $\bigcap_{x y} \vdash P:$ RSNI, we get an attacker $A$ such that $A: a t k$ and we need to prove $\vdash A[P]:$ SNI. Using that attacker $A$ on $\bigcap_{x y} \vdash P:$ RSS we get $\bigcap_{x y} \vdash A[P]:$ SS.
Now we can apply Theorem 53 (SS implies SNI) on $\bigcap_{x y} \vdash A[P]:$ SS and get $\bigcap_{x y} \vdash P:$ SNI.
Thus, we are finished.

And we can derive the following Corollary.
Corollary 7. If
(1) $\vdash \bigcap_{x y}: W F C$
(2) $\bigcap_{x y} \vdash P: S S$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
& I \bigcap_{x} \vdash P: S S \text { and } \\
& \text { II } \bigcap_{y} \vdash P: S S
\end{aligned}
$$

Proof. Unfolding $\bigcap_{x y} \vdash P: S S$ we have: $\forall \overline{\tau^{\sigma}} \in \operatorname{Beh}(P) . \forall \tau^{\sigma} \in \overline{\tau^{\sigma}} . \sigma \equiv S$. Choose an arbitrary $\overline{\tau^{\sigma}} \in \operatorname{Beh}(P)$. We know it is $\vdash \overline{\tau^{\sigma}}:$ safe.

By $\vdash \bigcirc_{x y}: W F C_{2}$ (Projection Preservation), we know that $\operatorname{Beh}_{x}^{\omega}(p)=\operatorname{Beh}_{x y}^{\omega}(p) \uparrow_{x y}^{x}$ and $\operatorname{Beh}_{y}^{\omega}(p)=\operatorname{Beh}_{x y}^{\omega}(p) \uparrow_{x y}^{y}$.

Furthermore, by definition of the projections $\uparrow_{x y}^{x}$ and $\uparrow_{x y}^{y}$ they only delete elements of a trace but never add observation to it.

Since $\vdash \overline{\tau^{\sigma}}:$ safe, we know by definition that $\vdash \overline{\tau^{\sigma}} \uparrow_{x y}^{x}:$ safe and $\vdash \overline{\tau^{\sigma}} \uparrow_{x y}^{y}:$ safe.
By Projection Preservation we know that $\overline{\tau^{\sigma}} \uparrow_{x y}^{x} \in \operatorname{Beh}_{x}^{\omega}(P)$ and $\overline{\tau^{\sigma}} \uparrow_{x y}^{y} \in \operatorname{Beh}_{y}^{\omega}(P)$.
Since the trace was arbitrarily chosen, we are finished.
Furthermore, if a compiler satisfies a combined contract $\bigcirc_{x y}$, than it also satisfies the two component contracts $\bigcirc_{x}$ and $\bigcirc_{y}$, which follows from Corollary 3 (Leakage Ordering and RSNIP) and Projection Preservation.

Corollary 8 (Combined Compiler Contract Security (RSNIP)).
(1) $\vdash \bigcirc_{x y}: W F C$ and
(2) $\bigcirc_{x y} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S N I P$
then
$I \bigcirc_{x} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S N I P$ and
II $\bigcirc_{y} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S N I P$
Proof. From $\vdash \bigcirc_{x y}: W F C$ (Projection Preservation) we get $\bigcirc_{x} \sqsubseteq \bigcirc_{x y}$ and $\bigcirc_{y} \sqsubseteq \bigcirc_{x y}$.
We can now apply Corollary 3 (Leakage Ordering and RSNIP) on $\bigcirc_{x y} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P$ and $\bigcirc_{x} \sqsubseteq \bigcirc_{x y}$ and $\bigcirc_{y} \sqsubseteq \bigcirc_{x y}$ respectively.

Thus, we are done.
We can state it for RSSP as well:
Corollary 9 (Combined Compiler Contract Security (RSSP)).
(1) $\vdash \bigcirc_{x y}: W F C$ and
(2) $\bigcirc_{x y} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P$
then
$I \bigcirc_{x} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P$ and
II $\bigcirc_{y} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P$
Proof. Assume a program p. By $\bigcirc_{x y} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P$ we know that there are only safe actions in $\operatorname{Beh}_{x y}^{\omega} \llbracket p \rrbracket$.

From $\vdash \bigcirc_{x y}: W F C$ (Projection Preservation) we get $\operatorname{Beh}_{x}^{\omega}\left(\llbracket p \rrbracket\right)=\operatorname{Beh}_{x y}^{\omega} \llbracket p \rrbracket \uparrow_{x y}^{x}$ and similar $\operatorname{Beh}_{y}^{\omega}\left(\llbracket p \rrbracket\right)=\operatorname{Beh}_{x y}^{\omega} \llbracket p \rrbracket \uparrow_{x y}^{x}$.

Thus, there are only safe actions in $\operatorname{Beh}_{x}^{\omega}\left(\llbracket p \rrbracket\right)$ and $\operatorname{Beh}_{y}^{\omega}\left(\llbracket p \rrbracket\right)$.
Since p was chosen arbitrarily, we are done.
Dually, if a program is insecure w.r.t. one of the components contracts, then it is insecure w.r.t. the composition contract as well.

Corollary 10 (Combined Compiler Contract Security Negative (RSNIP)).
(1) $\vdash \bigcirc_{x y}: W F C$ and
(2) $\bigcirc_{x} \not \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S N I P$ or $\bigcirc_{y} \not \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S N I P$

Then
$I \bigcirc_{x y} \not \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S N I P$

Proof. We do the proof for $\bigcirc_{x} \neq \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S N I P$.
The proof for $\bigcirc_{y} \neq \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S N I P$ is analogous.
Because of $\bigcirc_{x} \neq \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S N I P$ and $\bigcirc_{x} \subset \bigcirc_{x y}$ from Projection Preservation, we can apply Corollary 4 ([Leakage ordering and RSNIP Negative) and immediately get $\bigcirc_{x y} \neq \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S N I P$

Corollary 11 (Combined Compiler Contract Security Negative (RSSP)).
(1) $\vdash \bigcirc_{x y}: W F C$ and
(2) $\bigcirc_{x} \neq \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P$ or $\bigcirc_{y} \neq \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P$

Then

$$
I \bigcirc_{x y} \neq \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P
$$

Proof. We do the proof for $\bigcirc_{x} \neq \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P$.
The proof for $\bigcirc_{y} \neq \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P$ is analogous.
Because of $\bigcirc_{x} \neq \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P$, we know there exists a program $p$ such that $\bigcirc_{N S} \vdash p:$ RSS and $\bigcirc_{x} \neq \llbracket p \rrbracket:$ RSS.

That is, there is an unsafe action $\tau^{U}$ in the trace of $\llbracket p \rrbracket$.
From $\vdash \bigcirc_{x y}: W F C$ (Projection Preservation) we get $\operatorname{Beh}_{x}^{\omega}(\llbracket p \rrbracket)=\operatorname{Beh}_{x y}^{\omega} \llbracket p \rrbracket \rrbracket_{x y}^{x}$.
This means the unsafe action $\tau^{U}$ is part of the combined trace of $\llbracket p \rrbracket$ as well! Thus, $\bigcirc_{x y} \neq \llbracket p \rrbracket$ : RSS.

Since we have $\bigcirc_{N S} \vdash p:$ RSS and $\bigcirc_{x y} \neq \llbracket p \rrbracket:$ RSS we can conclude that $\bigcirc_{x y} \neq \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: R S S P$.

# X. 1 Using Relation Preservation on the Combination 

Next, we show how we can lift Relation Preservation of the combination to the reflexive transitive closure:

Lemma 72 (Comb: Steps of $\rrbracket_{x y}$ with safe observations preserve Safe-equivalence). If
(1) $\Sigma_{x y} \rrbracket_{x y}^{\bar{\tau}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger}$ and
(2) $\Sigma_{x y} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}$
(3) $\vdash \bar{\tau}:$ safe
(4) $\vdash \bigcirc_{x y}: W F C$

Then there exists $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$ such that
(1) $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime} \rrbracket_{x y}^{\bar{\tau}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$ and
(2) $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$

Proof. The proof proceeds by induction on $\Sigma_{x y} \rrbracket_{x y}^{\bar{\tau}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger}$ :
Rule xy:AM-Reflection
Then we have $\Sigma_{x y} \rrbracket_{x y}^{\bar{\tau}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger}$ where $\bar{\tau}=\varepsilon$ and $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger}=\Sigma_{x y}$.
Thus, we use Rule xy:AM-Reflection on $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}$ and get $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime} \rrbracket_{x y}^{\bar{\tau}^{\prime}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$, where where $\bar{\tau}^{\prime}=\varepsilon$ and $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}=\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}$.
Thus, $\bar{\tau}=\bar{\tau}^{\prime}$ trivially holds and $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$ holds by $\Sigma_{x y} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}$.
Rule xy:AM-silent
Then we have $\Sigma_{x y} \rrbracket_{x y}^{\bar{\tau}^{\prime}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger \dagger}$ and $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger \dagger} \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} \bigcirc_{x y}^{\varepsilon} \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger}$.

Applying the IH on $\Sigma_{x y} \Downarrow_{x y}^{\overline{\tau^{\prime}}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime} \Downarrow_{x y}^{\overline{\tau^{\prime \prime}}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime \prime} \\
& \Sigma_{x y}^{\tau \dagger} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime \prime} \\
& \quad \vdash \overline{\tau}^{\prime \prime}: \text { safe }
\end{aligned}
$$

Applying $\vdash \bigcap_{x y}: W F C_{3}$ (Relation Preservation) on $\Sigma_{x y}^{\tau \dagger} \stackrel{\epsilon}{\nvdash} \partial_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger}$ using $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger \dagger} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime \prime}$ and $\vdash \varepsilon:$ safe we get $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime \prime} \stackrel{\epsilon}{\nvdash} \partial_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{*}$ and $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{*}$.
Now choose $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{*}$.
We now use Rule xy:AM-silent and get $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime} \Downarrow_{x y}^{\overline{\tau}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$
$\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$ follows from $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{*}$ and $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}=\Sigma_{x y}^{*}$.
Rule xy:AM-Single
Then we have $\Sigma_{x y} \Downarrow_{x y}^{\overline{\tau^{\prime}}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger \dagger}$ and $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger \dagger} \stackrel{\tau^{\prime}}{\nvdash} \partial_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger}$.
Furthermore, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}=\bar{\Phi}_{x y} \cdot\langle\Omega, n\rangle \\
& \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}=\bar{\Phi}_{x y} \cdot\left\langle\Omega^{\prime}, n^{\prime}\right\rangle \\
& \text { find_fun }\left(\sigma^{\prime \prime}(\mathrm{pc})\right)=f \\
& \text { find_fun }\left(\sigma^{\prime}(\mathrm{pc})\right)=f^{\prime} \\
& \text { if } f==f^{\prime} \text { and } f \in \bar{I} \text { then } \tau^{t}=\epsilon \text { else } \tau^{t}=\tau^{t}
\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the IH on $\Sigma_{x y} \Downarrow_{x y}^{\overline{\tau^{\prime}}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime} \Downarrow_{x y}^{\overline{\tau^{\prime \prime}}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime \prime} \\
& \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger \dagger} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime \prime} \\
& \quad \vdash \overline{\tau}^{\prime \prime}: \text { safe }
\end{aligned}
$$

Applying $\vdash \bigcap_{x y}: W F C_{3}$ (Relation Preservation) on $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger \dagger} \stackrel{\tau^{\prime}}{\nvdash} \partial_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger}$ using $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger \dagger} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime \prime}$ and $\vdash \tau^{t}:$ safe (since $\vdash \bar{\tau}:$ safe) we get $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime \prime} \stackrel{\tau^{\prime}}{\nvdash} \partial_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{*}$ and $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{*}$.
Now choose $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{*}$.
We can now use Rule xy:AM-Single and get $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime} \Downarrow_{x y}^{\overline{\tau}} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$
$\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$ follows from $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger} \approx \Sigma_{x y}^{*}$ and $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}=\Sigma_{x y}^{*}$.

Lemma 73 (Comb : Low-equivalent programs have low-equivalent initial states).

$$
\forall P, P^{\prime} . \text { if } P={ }_{L} P^{\prime} \text { then } \Omega_{0}(P) \approx \Omega_{0}\left(P^{\prime}\right)
$$

Proof. Follows from the definition of initial states.

# X. 2 Deriving Relation Preservation generally 

Here we show how to derive Relation Preservation, a premise of $\vdash: W F C$, in a general fashion from additional assumptions about the source contracts
Definition $38\left(\approx_{x y}\right), \Sigma_{x y} \approx_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}$ iff $\Sigma_{x y} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x} \approx_{x} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x}$ and $\Sigma_{x y} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{y} \approx_{y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{y}$

Assumption 1 (Relation Preservation of x). If
(1) $\Sigma_{x}^{\dagger} \approx_{x} \Sigma_{x}^{\prime}$
(2) $\Sigma_{x}^{\dagger} \not \partial_{x} \Sigma_{x}^{\dagger \dagger}$
(3) $\vdash \tau:$ safe

Then there exists $\Sigma_{x}^{\prime \prime}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& I \Sigma_{x}^{\prime} \not \partial_{x} \Sigma_{x}^{\prime \prime} \\
& \text { II } \Sigma_{x}^{\dagger \dagger} \approx_{x} \Sigma_{x}^{\prime \prime}
\end{aligned}
$$

Assumption 2 (Relation Preservation of y). If
(1) $\Sigma_{y}^{\dagger} \approx_{y} \Sigma_{y}^{\prime}$
(2) $\Sigma_{y}^{\dagger} \not \partial_{y} \Sigma_{y}^{\dagger \dagger}$
(3) $\vdash \tau:$ safe

Then there exists $\Sigma_{y}^{\prime \prime}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& I \Sigma_{y}^{\prime} \not \partial_{y} \Sigma_{y}^{\prime \prime} \\
& \text { II } \Sigma_{y}^{\dagger \dagger} \approx_{y} \Sigma_{y}^{\prime \prime}
\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have two additional assumptions about the compatibility of the relations $\approx_{x}$ and $\approx_{y}$. These assumptions state that we can recompose the relation $\approx_{x y}$ from $\approx_{x}$ when doing a relation preserving step in the x semantics.

Assumption 3 (Compatibility of relation $\approx_{x}$ ). Let $\Sigma_{x y}=\bar{\Phi}_{x y} \cdot \Phi_{x y}$ and $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}=\bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\prime} \cdot \Phi_{x y}^{\prime}$. If
(1) $\Sigma_{x y} \approx_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}$ and
(2) $\Phi_{x y} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x} \not \bar{\Phi}_{x}^{\dagger}$
(3) $\Phi_{x y}^{\prime} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x} \not \partial_{x} \bar{\Phi}_{x}^{\prime \prime}$
(4) $\bar{\Phi}_{x}^{\dagger} \approx_{x} \bar{\Phi}_{x}^{\prime \prime}$ and
(5) $\bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\dagger} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x}=\bar{\Phi}_{x}^{\dagger}$ and $\bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\prime \prime} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x}=\bar{\Phi}_{x}^{\prime \prime}$
(6) $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger}=\bar{\Phi}_{x y} \cdot \bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\dagger}$ and $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}=\bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\prime} \cdot \bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$

Then
(1) $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger} \approx_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$

Assumption 4 (Compatibility of relation $\approx_{y}$ ). Let $\Sigma_{x y}=\bar{\Phi}_{x y} \cdot \Phi_{x y}$ and $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}=\bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\prime} \cdot \Phi_{x y}^{\prime}$. If
(1) $\Sigma_{x y} \approx_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}$ and
(2) $\Phi_{x y} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{y} \not \bar{\Phi}_{y}^{\dagger}$
(3) $\Phi_{x y}^{\prime} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{y} \not \partial_{y} \bar{\Phi}_{y}^{\prime \prime}$
(4) $\bar{\Phi}_{y}^{\dagger} \approx_{y} \bar{\Phi}_{y}^{\prime \prime}$ and
(5) $\bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\dagger} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{y}=\bar{\Phi}_{y}^{\dagger}$ and $\bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\prime \prime} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{y}=\bar{\Phi}_{y}^{\prime \prime}$
(6) $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger}=\bar{\Phi}_{x y} \cdot \bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\dagger}$ and $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}=\bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\prime} \cdot \bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$

Then
(1) $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger} \approx_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$

The safe condition is needed to get the equality of the traces. That is something that easily follows from low equivalence, since when a value is safe it can only depend on low equivalent values. Since they are low equivalent we are finished. This proof relies on Relation Preservation (+ Obs equal) and Confluence

Lemma 74 (Relation Preservation of $\bigcirc_{x y}$ ). If
(1) $\Sigma_{x y} \bigcirc_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger}$ and
(2) $\Sigma_{x y} \approx_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}$ and
(3) Assumption 1 (Relation Preservation of $x$ ) and Assumption 2 (Relation Preservation of y) and (4) $\vdash \tau:$ safe

Then
(1) $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime} \bigcirc_{x y}^{\prime} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$ and
(2) $\Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger} \approx_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$ and
(3) $\tau=\tau^{\prime}$

Proof. By $\Sigma_{x y} \approx_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}$, we know that $\Sigma_{x y} \cdot \mathbf{p c}=\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime} \cdot \mathbf{p c}$.
We start by inversion on $\Sigma_{x y} \bigcirc_{x y}^{\prime} \Sigma_{x y}^{\dagger}$ and $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime} \bigcirc_{x y}^{\prime} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$ :
Rule x-Rollback
Then we have $\Phi_{x y} \stackrel{\text { rlb }}{=} \bigcirc_{x y} \emptyset$ with $\Phi_{x y}^{0} \cdot n=0$ or $\vdash \Phi_{x y}^{*}:$ fin and $\Phi_{x y} \stackrel{\text { rlb }}{=} \bigcirc_{x y}^{\text {rlb }} \bigcirc_{x} \emptyset$.
By $\Sigma_{x y} \approx_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}$, we have $\Phi_{x y}^{\nu} \cdot n=\Phi_{x y}^{\nu} \cdot n=0$ or $\vdash \Phi_{x y}^{\nu \prime}:$ fin and $\vDash \Sigma_{x y}:$ fin (since there exists a step) implies $\vDash \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}:$ fin because of $\Sigma_{x y} \approx_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}$.

Furthermore, $\vDash \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}:$ fin and $\Sigma_{x y} \approx_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}$ together with $\Phi_{x y} \stackrel{\text { rlb }}{=} \bigcirc_{x}^{\text {rlb }} \bigcirc_{x} \emptyset$ implies $\vDash$ $\Sigma_{x y}^{\prime} \stackrel{\text { rlb }}{=}:$ fin and thus $\vDash \Phi_{x y}^{\prime} \stackrel{\text { rlb }}{=}:$ fin.

This means there necessarily exists a $\bar{\Phi}_{x}$ and $\tau^{\prime}$ such that $\Phi_{x y}^{\prime} \stackrel{\text { rlb }}{=} \bigcirc_{x}^{\tau^{\prime}} \bar{\Phi}_{x}$. By Assumption 1 (Relation Preservation of x ) we can then conclude that $\emptyset \approx_{x} \emptyset$ and $\tau \approx_{x} \mathrm{rlb}_{x}{ }^{x}$ and together with Assumption 3 (Compatibility of relation $\approx_{x}$ ) we get
$\Sigma_{x y}^{\tau} \approx_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$ and
$\tau \approx_{x y} \tau^{\prime}$ as required.
Rule y-Rollback
Analogous to above.
Rule Context-xy
Then we have $\Phi_{x y} \stackrel{\tau}{\bigcirc}_{x y} \bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\dagger}$.
We proceed by inversion $\Phi_{x y} \stackrel{\tau}{\bigcirc}_{x y} \bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\dagger}$ :
Rule x-step
Then we have $\Phi_{x y} \stackrel{\tau}{\bigcirc}_{x y} \stackrel{\tau}{\bigcirc}_{x} \bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\dagger} \stackrel{\tau}{\bigcirc}_{x y}^{\star}$.
Furthermore, we have $\Phi_{x y} \cdot \sigma(\mathbf{p c})=\Phi_{x y}^{\prime} \cdot \sigma(\mathbf{p c})$ because of $\Sigma_{x y} \approx_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime}$. That means the same instruction is executed.

Because of the definition of $\approx_{x y}$ we have $\Phi_{x y} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x} \approx_{x} \Phi_{x y}^{\prime} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x}$ as well. We can now use Assumption 1 (Relation Preservation of x ) on $\Phi_{x y} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x} \approx_{x} \Phi_{x y}^{\prime} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x}$ and $\Phi_{x y} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x} \stackrel{\ulcorner}{\Rightarrow}_{x} \bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\prime} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x}$ and $\vdash \tau$ : safe and get $\Phi_{x y}^{\prime} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x} \stackrel{\bar{\Phi}_{x}}{\Rightarrow}_{x} \bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\uparrow}$ and $\bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\uparrow} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x} \approx_{x} \bar{\Phi}_{x}^{\prime \prime}$.
Choose $\bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$ as $\bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\prime \prime} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x}=\bar{\Phi}_{x}^{\prime \prime}$
We now use Rule x-step with $\Phi_{x y}^{\prime} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x} \stackrel{\bar{\Phi}_{x}}{\Rightarrow}_{x}^{\prime \prime}$ and get $\Phi_{x y}^{\prime} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x} \stackrel{\ulcorner}{\Rightarrow}_{x y} \bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\prime \prime} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x}$.
It remains to show that $\Sigma_{x y}^{\uparrow} \approx_{x y} \Sigma_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$
Since only the topmost state changed, we need to show that $\bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\uparrow} \approx_{x y} \bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$.
We use Assumption 3 (Compatibility of relation $\approx_{x}$ ) on $\bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\uparrow} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x} \approx_{x} \bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\prime \prime} \upharpoonright_{x y}^{x}$ since we fulfill all conditions and get $\bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\uparrow} \approx_{x y} \bar{\Phi}_{x y}^{\prime \prime}$ and are finished.
Rule y-step
Analogous to above using Assumption 2 (Relation Preservation of y) and Assumption 4 (Compatibility of relation $\approx_{y}$ ).

# Y WFC for all combinations 

Here, we argue why all our combined contracts presented are WFC.
In general, Confluence follows from the correct instantiation of the metaparameter $Z$. Our AM semantics delegate back to the non-speculative semantics in all cases not related to speculation. Since the non-speculative semantics is deterministic, all the rules delegating back are confluent. The only difference in the execution can appear if speculation is started. However, then the metaparamter restricts the no-branching rule of the other semantics part of the combination and it cannot be used. Thus, speculation is always started and only one rule is possible, contradicting the assumption of Confluence.

For Projection Preservation, we refer to [24] since the proofs are virtually the same. Intuitively this follows from the structure of our semantics. We never forget a speculative transaction because of the metaparameter Z restriction. Thus, no actions are forgotten.

For Relation Preservation, we on our general construction in Appendix X.2, where we need to fulfil the assumptions made, which we will provide now:
$\bigwedge_{\mathrm{B}}$ The lemmas needed are [46, Lemma L.6]
$\bigwedge_{J}$ The lemmas needed are Lemma 16 ( $\$$ Steps of $\cup_{j}$ with safe observations preserve Safeequivalence).
$\bigwedge_{\$}$ The lemmas needed are Lemma 10 (Steps of $\cup_{\$}$ with safe observations preserve Safeequivalence).
$\bigwedge_{\mathrm{R}}$ The lemmas needed are Lemma 19 (R: Steps of $\cup_{\mathrm{R}}$ with safe observations preserve Safeequivalence).
$\bigwedge_{\mathrm{SLS}}$ The lemmas needed are Lemma 13 (SLS: Steps of $\cup_{\mathrm{SLS}}$ with safe observations preserve Safe-equivalence).
Now for the compatibility lemmas between $\approx_{x}$ and $\approx_{y}$ Assumption 3 (Compatibility of relation $\approx_{x}$ ) and Assumption 4 (Compatibility of relation $\approx_{y}$ ).

First, let us quickly note that the relation $\approx$ is the same for $\mathrm{B}, \mathrm{J}, \mathrm{S}$ and SLS.
Only for R , we have the additional constraint that the Rsb $\mathbb{R}$ is related.
Thus, for all combinations not involving $\bigwedge_{\mathrm{ij}}$, the compatibility lemma trivial holds since there is no difference between $\approx_{x}$ and $\approx_{x y}$.

For combinations involving $\bigcap_{0}$, we know that when a step of the other source semantics is happening, the Rsb $\mathbb{R}$ is not changed. Thus, it is also easy to reinstate $\approx_{x y}$ in those cases.

Thus, we fulfil all assumptions to derive Relation Preservation for all our source contracts

# Z Independence Results 

Here, we describe our Independence results.
We first list injlnst( $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket$ ) and speclnst( $\bigcap$ ) of our compilers and and spec. semantics (Table 3).

![table_5](table_5)


![table_6](table_6)

Table 3. The type of instructions inserted by our compilers and the speculative instructions for the semantics.

A (static) jmp instruction is local and produces no observation. For combined semantics, we use the union of the speculation instructions.

Table 4 describes in which cases (Syn.) Independence applies to the different spec. semantics we define.

If there is an entry for compiler $\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket$ in column $\bigcap_{y}$ then we can show the following (Syn.) Independence statement: $\bigcap_{y} \vdash \llbracket \cdot \rrbracket: I$.

Adding a fence to $\llbracket \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}$ to get $\llbracket \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l f}$ allows us to achieve Independence w.r.t to $\bigcap_{0,5}$. We could do the same for $\llbracket \rrbracket_{0}^{\prime p l}$, however, we cannot combine $\bigcap_{0}$ with $\bigcap_{0,5}$ due to limitations in the combination framework.

We want to note that for $\bigcap_{j}$ speculation happens only on indirect jumps, while the retpoline compilers only insert direct jumps. If a jump is direct or indirect can be seen statically by inspection of the code. That is why we have for example $B+\gamma \vdash \llbracket \rrbracket_{j}^{\prime p l}: S I$.

![img-68.jpeg](img-68.jpeg)
![img-69.jpeg](img-69.jpeg)

Table 4. Lists of Secure compilers and how they attain Independence for our semantics $\vdash \llbracket \llbracket$ : SL. SI means by Syntactic Independence, I means by proving Independence and $X$ means that Independence is not possible. For $\llbracket \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{L S L H}$ we use a different observer named the $c t+v l$ observer.

Technically, we have that Syntactic Independence does not hold for $\llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{r p l}$ w.r.t. $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}}$, since ret instructions are added. However, the Independence proof is a consequence of Corollary 5 (Self Independence) and $\llbracket \llbracket \rrbracket_{\mathrm{B}}^{r p l} \vdash R S S P$ and this extends to all the combined semantics using $\bigcap_{\mathrm{B}}$ as well.

# AB How instantiate Labels: Or how to link the program to run it 

In the syntax of the program we have abstract labels, that annotate each instructions and are used for jmp instructions. For example jmp $l$ (where $l$ is an abstract label of the program) should jump to that location in the program. This is done because when we compile the source language and insert a countermeasure we would need to shift all instruction numbers by one (i.e. if we insert a fence). That is why we have these abstract labels.

A second reason is that attacker and component define their functions. But they do not know which instruction number the other uses. We cannot allow clashes because otherwise it is not defined what jmp 2 means, when there are multiple instructions it can belong to.

While our semantics works on those abstract labels, we could instantiate these labels to concrete values, e.g., numbers. This is essentially modelling the work of the linker and there are some pitfalls that we need to consider. For example, since we want to prove something about the security of our compilers, we need a cross language trace relation $\approx$ that relates source and target traces. Thus, we need to somehow relate the concrete locations between source and target program.

The labels $l$ are drawn from a countable infinite set $L$.
For the remainder of this technical report, we will not use the exact details of these labels.

AB.0.1 An example. First, we need to plug together all the different functions of the attacker and the component. We assume that each instruction has a unique label, which is reasonable. Otherwise, we would rename certain labels.

Let us look at an image of two functions $f$ and $g$ with their instructions and their respective order.

![img-72.jpeg](img-72.jpeg)

Note, that this is not the control flow graph of the program. Even if function $g$ would contains a loop or an if statement the resulting diagram would be the same. We are only interested in the program order of the instructions itself.

Just looking at the functions in isolation, we can see that the labels form a total order. However, looking at the whole program together, it is course not a total order. The instructions between the two functions are not related, e.g. , $i 1<j 1$ or $j 1<i 1$ does not hold. This means these functions form chains in the partial order of the whole program.

AB.0.2 The algorithm. What we want is a function mapping the abstract labels of the program to natural numbers. This function should be isomorphic.

First, we know that the set of labels of a program $L_{P}$ is finite because we do not have infinite programs. Every finite order has a least element and is in fact a well order

This means we can just take a totally ordered set of natural numbers ordered by $<$ that has the same cardinality as the set of labels used in the program.

This algorithm computes a bijection between the program labels ordered by an initial segment of the natural numbers.

We take a random label in the program. Each label belongs to one function in the program. Since the functions itself are total ordered and are finite, we know that there is a least element in that total order. We essentially 'climb down' the chain as the starting point. This ensures that we do not end up in situations like this for some function $f$ :

```
5 : jmp 1_1
3 : ...
4 : load eax, 2
```

The algorithm ensures that the full chain / function is consistent in the numbering.
Then we 'climb up the chain by using the definition of cover (i.e. the smallest element that is bigger in the total order) and assign natural numbers in increasing order to those labels. After we are done with this chain, the algorithm will select the next one.

The map $\mathcal{L}$ is a partial function from abstract labels to natural numbers. However, we know that the function will be total for all labels used in the program by construction.

```
Algorithm 1 Computing the label map
    Input
        (P, R)The partial order defined of the program where P includes all labels used in the
        program
        n A natural number n used as initial seed to generate the successor set of n .
    Output
        \(\mathcal{L} \quad\) A map from labels to natural numbers
        \(N \quad\) The finite successor set of N
    procedure \(\operatorname{Euclid}(a, b)\)
        \(N=\emptyset\)
        \(\mathcal{L}=\emptyset\)
        while !empty \((P)\) do
            \(x \leftarrow \operatorname{rand}(P)\)
            \(l \leftarrow\) least_element \((x)\)
            while \(\operatorname{cover}(l, R) \neq l\) do
                \(P \leftarrow P \backslash l\)
                \(\mathcal{L} \leftarrow \mathcal{L}[l \mapsto n]\)
                \(N \leftarrow N \cup n\)
                \(n \leftarrow n+1\)
            end while
        end while
        return \((\mathcal{L}, N)\)
    end procedure
```

AB.0.3 Why we use the successor set of $N$. Note that instead of adding 1 to n in Algorithm 1 we could have increased $n$ arbitrarily. Furthermore, we need to use this algorithm for both the source program and the compiled program. Because the compiler can add instructions into the program.

AB.0.4 Computing the initial partial order of the whole program. To use our algorithm, we need to give it as input the partial order of the program $P$.
W.l.o.g we assume that the labels used per function are disjoined. We can define the partial order of the program P by the sum of all total orders defined by the functions appearing in the program.

Definition 39. $\sum_{\left(\mathcal{P}_{l}, \mathcal{T}_{l}\right) \in\{P, \bar{F}, P, \bar{I}\}}\left(\mathcal{P}_{l}, \mathcal{T}_{l}\right)$
Now it remains to show, how we can compute the total orders for each function.
We give an example how to do it for function. First, we map all entry points of functions into a set S. First, lookup the function $f$ in the function map $F(f)=l$. This $l$ is the first instruction of the function. A program is a sequence of labelled instructions. We iterate this sequence until the function is finished. This means until we find a label that is in the set of function entry points. so $l: i ; l_{i}: i^{\prime} ; p 2$ we add the edge $\left(l, l_{i}\right) \cup R$ and unfold the sequence further.

When then take the transitive closure and obtain $R^{*}$.

# AB. 1 The abstract label semantics 

Instead of using the instantiation, we just use the abstract labels.
(Registers) $x \in$ Regs (Labels) $l \in L \quad$ (Nats) $n \in \mathbb{N} \cup\{\perp\} \quad$ (Values) $v \in$ Vals $=\mathbb{N} \cup\{\perp\} \cup L$

# AB.1.1 Expression Evaluation. 

![img-73.jpeg](img-73.jpeg)

BinOp and unop now take a natural number(extended with $\perp$ ). Lookup can return a label

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { (Assign) } \\
& p\left(a_{v}(\mathrm{pc})\right)=x \leftarrow e \quad x \neq \mathrm{pc} \\
& \overline{C ; \overline{B_{v}} ;\left\langle p, M_{v}, a_{v}\right\rangle} \xrightarrow{C ; \overline{B_{v}} ;\left\langle m, a_{v}[\mathrm{pc} \mapsto \operatorname{inc}(\mathrm{pc}), x \mapsto a_{v} \vDash e \downarrow v]\right\rangle}
\end{aligned}
$$

Essentially we could decide to have a static semantics using labels and a run time semantics, where we instantiate all the labels. We define the semantics on the abstract labels. However, since we defined how we can instantiate these labels we try to keep this abstract. The difference is really just notational. That is why we have the function inc defined:

$$
\operatorname{inc}(\mathrm{pc})= \begin{cases}\mathrm{pc}+1 & \text { if } \mathrm{pc} \in \mathbb{N} \\ \operatorname{succ}(\mathrm{pc}) & \text { if } \mathrm{pc} \in L\end{cases}
$$

where $\operatorname{succ}(l)$ computes the cover of the label $l$. Since the cover of a label $l$ can be the label itself, i.e. at the end of a function when there is no return (which is strange in itself.). We need to annotate this with a special symbol (similar to $\perp$ for nats), recording that the program is now in a stuck state.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& p\left(a_{v}(\mathrm{pc})\right)=\text { load } x, e \stackrel{(\text { Load })}{x} x \neq \mathrm{pc} \quad a_{v} \vDash e \downarrow n \\
& \overline{C ; \overline{B_{v}} ;\left\langle p, M_{v}, a_{v}\right\rangle} \xrightarrow{\text { load } n} C ; \overline{B_{v}} ;\left\langle M_{v}, a_{v}\left[\mathrm{pc} \mapsto a_{v}(\mathrm{pc})+1, x \mapsto M_{v}^{\mathrm{L}}(n)\right]\right\rangle \\
& p\left(a_{v}(\mathrm{pc})\right)=\text { store } x, e \quad a_{v} \vDash e \downarrow n \\
& \overline{C ; \overline{B_{v}} ;\left\langle p, M_{v}, a_{v}\right\rangle} \xrightarrow{\text { store } n} C ; \overline{B_{v}} ;\left\langle M_{v}^{\mathrm{L}}\left[n \mapsto a_{v}(x)\right], a_{v}\left[\mathrm{pc} \mapsto a_{v}(\mathrm{pc})+1\right]\right\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

Note that in both rules the expression $e$ needs to evaluate to a natural number $n$. This implicitly means that there are no labels $l$ in the expression $e$.

Let us explain why we forbid labels in the expression $e$ of store and loads. First of all, labels are not instantiated in our semantics so a store location like $l$ is not in the domain of the memory.

Of course, this argument does not hold if one simply instantiates the semantics. We will explain this detail in Appendix AB. 2 where we argue that we still should forbid labels from appearing as store and load locations.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& p\left(a_{v}(\mathrm{pc})\right)=\mathrm{imp} e \quad \stackrel{(\mathrm{imp})}{a_{v}} e \stackrel{(\mathrm{~s}}{=} \ell \\
& \text { find_fun }\left(a_{v}(\mathrm{pc})\right)=f \quad \text { find_fun }(\ell)=f^{\prime} \quad \text { C.intfs } \vdash f, f^{\prime}: \text { internal } \\
& \overline{C ; \overline{B_{v}} ;\left\langle p, M_{v}, a_{v}\right\rangle} \xrightarrow{\text { jcc } f} C ; \overline{B_{v}} ;\left\langle m, a[\mathrm{pc} \mapsto \ell]\right\rangle
\end{aligned}
$$

Here the expression $e$ needs to evaluate to a label. So eiher $e$ is just a label $l$ or is a register $r$ containing a label $l$. The second case is actually called an indirect jump (relevant for SPectre V2) because the label is indirectly stored in the register. Some CPUs allow jmp [ $n$ ] where [ $n$ ] means the

value stored at memory address $n$. We do not have that but can simulate it by load $r, n$ followed by jmp $r$. Furthermore, using the gcc flag -mindirect-branch-register prohibits the use indirect jumps using memory and essentially does a rewrite like we do.

In Appendix AB. 2 we argue why one should not allow natural numbers as targets for jumps in the instantiated semantics.

# AB. 2 Using the Instantiation : Semantics 

We have shown the changes to the semantics when one uses the abstract labels. However, we can define the semantics using the instantiation of the labels using our computed $\mathcal{L}$. This means that all labels are resolved before/during the execution of the program.

For example, resolving the labels at run-time means that we add an additional rule the expression evaluation.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sigma, \mathcal{L} \triangleright e \downarrow v \\
& \frac{(\text { E-label })}{\mathcal{L}(l)=n}{\sigma_{v}, \mathcal{L} \triangleright l \downarrow n}
\end{aligned}
$$

This is similar to a virtual memory address lookup.
AB.2.1 Store instructions. In Appendix AB. 1 we explained why the expression $e$ of store and loads cannot contain any labels. In the instantiation however, labels are resolved to natural numbers, so they could be used as store and load locations.

However, we argue that they still should not be used.
Consider the small program and two to possible instantiations according to our algorithm :

```
1_1 : load r1,
    1_x
1_2 : store x,
    1_3
1_3 : store x,
    100
```

```
1 : load r1, 8
2 : store x, 3
3 : store x, 100
```

Listing 4. Code on the left and the instantiated code on the right for different instantiations.
In the program, we have a load instruction in Line 1 loading from the location of label $l_{x}$ and a store instruction in Line 2 that stores to location $l_{3}$. See that the load instruction now nondeterministically chooses the location from memory dependent on the layout the linker created. Second, for the store instruction in Line 2, the store location can overlap with the store in Line 3. Again, this behaviour depends on the layout of the program which the linker chooses. Most importantly, both of these behaviours are probably not intended by the programmer. Thereby, we do not allow them.

That is why we will not allow abstract labels as destination and sources for store and load instructions.

AB.2.2 Jmp instructions. Similar for jmp instructions, allowing natural numbers to be used as jump targets is a bad idea as well. Consider this program:

![table_8](table_8)


![table_9](table_9)

In Appendix AB.2.2 the jump actually resolves. However, in Appendix AB.2.2 the jump does not resolve because there exists no instruction at location 5!

Again, the programmer relies on the layout of the program, which the linker decides.

AB.2.3 Using the instantiation: Changes to the Cross-Language relation. Even though we use the abstract labels in the semantics. It is possible to use the instantiation as well. At run-time the $\mathcal{L}$ would be used to resolve all labels in the program.

However, one needs to be careful with the cross-language relation. In the instantiation of the labels we have observations like pc $n$ for jmp instructions. Since we need to relate source and target traces, we need to very careful here.

Essentially what we do is a reverse lookup

![table_10](table_10)

Listing 5. Code on the left and the compiled program with a countermeasure on the right.
Lets assume we have an instantiation of the abstract labels according to our algorithm starting at 1. Here, we have the observations pc 3 and pc 4 when executing the jmp instruction in source and target program. However, these observations should be related, because they actually jump to the same instruction. The mismatch happens, because of the added countermeasure by the compiler.

So to relate source and target traces, we use the $\mathcal{L}^{-1}$ and $\mathcal{L}^{-1}$ to do a reverse lookup and check if they map to the same abstract label

$$
\frac{\mathcal{L}^{-1}(n)=\mathcal{L}^{-1}\left(\mathrm{n}^{\prime}\right)}{p c n^{t} \stackrel{A}{\approx} p c \mathrm{n}^{\prime t}}
$$

(Action Relation - pcObs)

So even though we have pc 3 and pc 4 they are related by the trace relation because $\mathcal{L}^{-1}(3)=l_{3}$ and $\mathcal{L}^{-1}(4)=l_{3}$ !

# AB. 3 Lifting the restriction on the jumps 

A jump instruction like jmp $l_{1}+2$ is not allowed right now. Here we explain, how one could lift this restriction

Use the partial order of the source $\mathcal{L}$ to resolve jump targets in the target language. See this example

![table_11](table_11)

```
1_1 : jmp 1_1 + 2
1_2 : store x, e
1_2' : spbarr
1_3 : load eax, 2
```

Listing 6. Code on the left and the compiled program with a countermeasure on the right.
We expect the program in the source to jump to $l_{3}$. However in the target language, the compiler added a barrier instruction. Thus the target code could jump to $l_{2}^{\prime}$. To remediate the situation, we need to think how we can resolve $l_{1}+2$.

Naively, we could use our label bijection to get $\mathcal{L}\left(l_{1}\right)+2$. Assuming our order starts at 1 , this would resolve to 3 . Computing in the target, we get $\mathcal{L}\left(l_{1}\right)+2=3$. In this case $\mathcal{L}\left(l_{1}\right)=\mathcal{L}\left(l_{1}\right)$. This is generally not the case. Think about it if the jmp was after the barrier instruction. This would shift the target level jump by 1 for example.

They both jump to instruction. This then points to the load instruction in the src and the barrier instruction in the target which is a mismatch that we do not want.

Instead, we transform the computation into the partial order domain: $l_{1}+2=\operatorname{succ}\left(\operatorname{succ}\left(l_{1}\right)\right)$. This computation returns a label instead of a natural number. In this case $l_{3}$. On which we now can apply the labelmap of the source. $\mathcal{L}\left(l_{1}\right)=3$

Note that we applied the success function on the partial order of the source program. If we use the partial order of the target program we would get $\operatorname{succ}\left(\operatorname{succ}\left(l_{1}\right)\right)=l_{2^{\prime}}$ and we gained nothing because that still not what we want. However, we could use the partial order of the source program to compute $\operatorname{succ}\left(\operatorname{succ}\left(l_{1}\right)\right)=l_{3}$. On which we now apply the labelmap of the target program: $\mathcal{L}\left(l_{3}\right)=4$.

So we compute the successor label using the partial order of the source program and then apply the label map of either source or target language. The trick was to interpret + in the abstract domain of the partial order and to use the partial order of the source in the target as well! $\mathcal{L}(1+\mathrm{n})$, where + means the successor of the label. We think that this is a model of relocations that the linker applies when linking code together.

abstract:
Mainstream compilers implement different countermeasures to prevent specific
classes of speculative execution attacks. Unfortunately, these countermeasures
either lack formal guarantees or come with proofs restricted to speculative
semantics capturing only a subset of the speculation mechanisms supported by
modern CPUs, thereby limiting their practical applicability. Ideally, these
security proofs should target a speculative semantics capturing the effects of
all speculation mechanisms implemented in modern CPUs. However, this is
impractical and requires new secure compilation proofs to support additional
speculation mechanisms. In this paper, we address this problem by proposing a
novel secure compilation framework that allows lifting the security guarantees
provided by Spectre countermeasures from weaker speculative semantics (ignoring
some speculation mechanisms) to stronger ones (accounting for the omitted
mechanisms) without requiring new secure compilation proofs. Using our lifting
framework, we performed the most comprehensive security analysis of Spectre
countermeasures implemented in mainstream compilers to date. Our analysis spans
9 different countermeasures against 5 classes of Spectre attacks, which we
proved secure against a speculative semantics accounting for five different
speculation mechanisms.
